For Newman they were more than a scholarly task. His study of the Arian crisis had produced his first book, The Arians of the Fourth Century, and fed the thinking he later traced in the Apologia. In the revision of 1881 he relaxed the strict literalism the Oxford translators had practised, so that the English reads more freely while keeping close to the Greek.

No. 33 of Lérins Newman, in its second part on the Catholic years 1848–1885, sets the text from the uniform edition’s 1903 impression of the revised translation. Newman’s prefatory notices and his footnotes, which form a commentary in their own right, are kept as he left them. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Athanasius, the councils of the fourth century and Newman’s work as translator over forty years, and explanatory notes on the persons, creeds and Greek terms of the controversy. The companion volume of Newman’s annotations is No. 34.

title: Select Treatises of St. Athanasius, Volume 2
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The second volume of Newman’s Athanasius is his own reference book to the Arian controversy, a series of short articles on its persons, doctrines and Greek terms, arranged in alphabetical order.
description: Select Treatises of St. Athanasius, Volume 2 contains no translation. It is a set of annotations on the treatises in Volume 1, arranged alphabetically in two series. The first takes theological subjects, among them Adam, the Arians, the Vicarious Atonement, the Coinherence, Deification, Economical Language, the Incarnation, the Blessed Mary, Private Judgment, the Rule of Faith, the Scripture Canon, Tradition and the Holy Trinity in Unity, with entries on figures such as Arius, Eusebius, Marcellus, Meletius, Paul of Samosata and Sabellius. The second takes Greek terms of the controversy, from agenneton and homoousios to ousia, monogenes, Logos and Theotokos. Much of this material grew out of the long notes Newman had attached to his Oxford translation of the 1840s, gathered into one place for the revised edition of 1881.

The volume is Newman’s most compact statement of patristic theology as he understood it at the end of his life. In short articles he sets out what Athanasius and the other Fathers meant by their key words, how the Nicene terms came to be fixed, and how the controversy bore on later questions of tradition, development and the rule of faith. The entries on Scripture and Tradition show his long interest in how doctrine is handed on. Scholarship on the Fathers has moved on since 1881 on many points of text and dating. The annotations remain a guide to the vocabulary of fourth-century theology, and to the way Newman himself read it after half a century of study.

No. 34 of Lérins Newman, the companion to No. 33 in the second part of the collection, the Catholic years 1848–1885, follows the 1903 impression of the uniform edition. Newman’s articles, his cross-references and his Greek terms appear as he left them. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the history of the annotations and on how to use them with the treatises, and explanatory notes that identify the Fathers, councils and heretics Newman cites and render his Greek and Latin terms for readers who do not have those languages.

title: Meditations and Devotions
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The prayers and meditations Newman wrote for his own use and for his community, gathered after his death, including the meditation on God creating each person for “some definite service.”
description: Meditations and Devotions was edited in 1893 by Father William P. Neville, Newman’s secretary in his last years, from papers that Newman had meant in part for a “Year-Book of Devotion” he never completed. The book is dedicated to the boys of the Oratory School. It has three parts. The first holds meditations on the Litany of Loretto for the month of May, arranged under the Immaculate Conception, the Annunciation, Our Lady’s Dolours and the Assumption, with a memorandum on the Immaculate Conception and a novena and litany of St. Philip Neri. The second gives meditations on the Stations of the Cross, twelve meditations and intercessions for Good Friday, meditations for eight days and a series of litanies. The third is a set of meditations on Christian doctrine, with a short visit to the Blessed Sacrament.

These pages show Newman praying rather than arguing. The Marian meditations are short readings for each day of May. The meditations on Christian doctrine, on hope in God, on God and the soul, on sin, on the Holy Ghost and on the Sacred Heart, are written in the first person and addressed to God. The meditation on hope in God as Creator says that “God has created me to do Him some definite service,” and it has become one of the most quoted passages Newman wrote. The prayers have been used by Catholics and by readers of other traditions since the book appeared. The volume gives the inner life behind the public controversies of his Catholic years, in his own voice.

No. 35 of Lérins Newman, in its second part, the Catholic years 1848–1885, takes its text from Neville’s edition in the 1907 impression, with his dedication and prefatory notice. Newman’s own notes, and the few added by his first editor, are kept as they were left. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the papers, what can be known of their dates and Neville’s work in arranging them. Their explanatory notes cover the litanies, feasts and Latin texts the meditations use and the devotions of the Oratory that they assume.

title: Faith and Prejudice, and Other Sermons
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Nine sermons Newman wrote out as a Catholic that went unpublished in his lifetime, seven of them from his first weeks of preaching in Birmingham in 1848.
description: Faith and Prejudice, and Other Sermons was edited by the Birmingham Oratory and first published in 1956. Its introduction explains that of the sermons Newman composed as a Catholic whose autographs survive, only these nine seem to have escaped publication. Seven were preached at St. Chad’s Cathedral, Birmingham, in the early months of 1848, when Newman was living at Maryvale and walked in to preach, the last of them on the third Sunday of Lent. They include “The Omnipotence of God the Reason for Faith and Hope,” “Preparation for the Judgment,” “Prejudice and Faith,” “Surrender to God” and “Our Lady in the Gospel.” The eighth, “Stewards and also Sons of God,” dates from July 1870, and the ninth, “The Infidelity of the Future,” from the opening of St. Bernard’s Seminary at Olton in October 1873.

The 1848 sermons are among the first Newman preached in England as a Catholic priest, weeks after his return from Rome, and they show him speaking to a Catholic congregation in a manufacturing town for the first time. He wrote them out in full and numbered them, as he had done as an Anglican, and they treat the themes of his Oxford pulpit, faith, judgment, grace and the world, from his new position. “The Infidelity of the Future” is the best known. Preached to seminarians, it warns that the coming age will face unbelief of a kind the Church has not met before, and it is often quoted for what the introduction calls its “grim forecast of the future course of unbelief.”

No. 36 of Lérins Newman closes the second part of the collection, the Catholic years 1848–1885. The text follows the Birmingham Oratory’s 1956 edition, with its introduction on the manuscripts and the occasions, and with Newman’s own notes as he left them. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction placing the sermons in the founding of the English Oratory and in the Catholic Birmingham of 1848 and 1873. Their explanatory notes cover the Scripture, the liturgical seasons and the persons the sermons name, and compare passages with the Anglican sermons on the same themes.

title: Prefaces and Occasional Writings
subtitle: Froude’s Remains, the Library of the Fathers, the Lives of the English Saints and other pieces
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The shorter pieces Newman wrote for other men’s books and for the reviews, from his preface to Hurrell Froude’s Remains in 1838 to his last article, written at eighty-four.
description: This volume gathers six of Newman’s shorter writings, each too brief for a book of its own, in the order he wrote them. The Preface to the Remains of Richard Hurrell Froude (1838), written with John Keble, defends the printing of their dead friend’s private journal and letters. The prefaces to the Oxford Library of the Fathers introduce its volumes of Cyril of Jerusalem, Cyprian and Chrysostom. Three Lives of hermits, Gundleus, Edelwald and Bettelin, come from the Lives of the English Saints he projected at Littlemore in 1843.

From the Catholic years come the memoir of his Oriel pupil and lifelong friend Henry Wilberforce (1873), the Prefatory Notice to William Palmer’s Notes of a Visit to the Russian Church (1882), the journal of an Oxford fellow who went to Petersburg in 1840 to ask the Orthodox for communion, and The Development of Religious Error (1885), Newman’s reply to A. M. Fairbairn’s charge that his defence of faith rested on scepticism, with the sections he added in 1890. Together they follow Newman from the Oxford Movement to his last years, as editor, biographer and controversialist.

No. 37 of Lérins Newman, the first title in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse, prints only what is Newman’s. The Froude preface, written with Keble, is presented as the work of both, and the books these pieces introduced are not reprinted. Each is set from the text kept in the site’s library under its own heading. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the six pieces and their occasions, and explanatory notes on the people, places and books they name. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them.

title: Historical Tracts of St. Athanasius
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The papers Athanasius gathered to defend himself against the Arians, from the letters of councils and popes to the soldiers breaking into his church, edited by Newman for the Oxford Library of the Fathers.
description: Historical Tracts of St. Athanasius was published at Oxford in 1843 as a volume of the Library of the Fathers, with a preface signed by John Henry Newman on 4 December of that year. It gathers eight works of Athanasius, Archbishop of Alexandria. They are the Encyclical Epistle, the Apology against the Arians with its documents from the Council of Egypt, Pope Julius, the Council of Sardica and the Council of Tyre, the Encyclical to the Bishops of Egypt and Libya, the Apology to the Emperor Constantius, the Apology for his Flight, the letter to Serapion on the death of Arius, the letter to the Monks, and the History of the Arians, whose opening is lost.

These tracts are a chief first-hand record of the Arian controversy in the decades after Nicaea. In them Athanasius answers the charges laid against him by the Meletians and at Tyre, prints the letters that cleared him, and tells how he was driven from Alexandria again and again. The Apology for his Flight describes the soldiers of Duke Syrianus breaking into the Church of Theonas while he sat on his throne there. Newman’s preface is a long study of the chronology of the period, which he warns can be no more than hypothetical, beginning with the intervention of Pope Julius in the affairs of the East. Newman had written on the Arians since 1833, and Athanasius remained central to his work for the rest of his life.

This is No. 38 of Lérins Newman, in the part for collected essays, sketches and verse. Newman edited the volume and wrote its preface. The English translation itself is acknowledged in that preface to the Rev. Miles Atkinson, late Fellow of Lincoln College, and is given here as the work of both men in their parts. The text is set from the 1843 volume. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction to the tracts, their history and Newman’s work on them, with explanatory notes on persons, councils and dates. The notes of the 1843 edition are kept as they were left.

title: Essays Critical and Historical, Volume 1
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Nine essays from Newman’s Oxford years, on poetry, rationalism, tradition and the prospects of the English Church, reprinted by him in 1871 with notes on where his mind had since changed.
description: Essays Critical and Historical, Volume 1, opens the two volumes in which John Henry Newman collected his longer articles in 1871, with a dedication to William Froude dated 1 August 1871. It begins with Poetry, with reference to Aristotle’s Poetics, written in 1828 for the London Review. Tract 73, On the Introduction of Rationalistic Principles into Revealed Religion, follows, with its discussion of Thomas Erskine and of Jacob Abbott’s Corner Stone. The rest are reviews from the British Critic of 1836 to 1840. They are Apostolical Tradition, the Fall of de la Mennais, Palmer on Faith and Unity, the Theology of St. Ignatius, Prospects of the Anglican Church, the Anglo-American Church, and Selina, Countess of Huntingdon.

The essays show Newman at work as a leading writer of the Oxford Movement, setting the Church of England’s claim to be part of the Catholic Church against its history and its critics. They take up the authority of tradition, the danger he saw in judging revelation by private reason, and the fortunes of other bodies, from de la Mennais in France to the Episcopal Church in America. In 1871 Newman, by then a Catholic, chose to reprint them without alteration rather than leave others to reprint them without comment. His Advertisement explains the plan, and the notes he added to several essays answer what he no longer held. A reader therefore has his first thoughts and his second side by side.

This is No. 39 of Lérins Newman, and the first of the two volumes of Essays Critical and Historical in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. The text follows the 1871 edition, with the dedication, the Advertisement and the later notes in their places. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project contribute a new introduction placing each essay in the years from 1828 to 1840, and explanatory notes on the books reviewed and the persons named. Newman’s own notes, early and late, are kept as he left them, so that both layers of his text remain visible.

title: Essays Critical and Historical, Volume 2
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The last of Newman’s Anglican journalism, from the British Critic of 1840 to 1842, together with his Catholic review of Keble’s Lyra Innocentium and the notes he added in 1871.
description: Essays Critical and Historical, Volume 2, continues the collection John Henry Newman made in 1871. Six of its seven essays first appeared in the British Critic between January 1840 and April 1842. They are the Catholicity of the Anglican Church, the Protestant Idea of Antichrist, Milman’s View of Christianity, the Reformation of the Eleventh Century, Private Judgment, and a study of John Davison, the Oriel divine. The seventh, John Keble, is a review of Keble’s Lyra Innocentium dated June 1846, written after Newman had become a Catholic. A Postscript prints William Palmer of Worcester College’s disavowal of opinions that Newman had ascribed to him in the first volume.

The Catholicity of the Anglican Church, of January 1840, is the fullest statement in these volumes of the claim that the English Church is a true part of the Catholic Church despite its separation from Rome. The Antichrist essay argues against the Protestant reading of the Pope as Antichrist. The review of Milman, the essay on the reforming popes of the eleventh century and the essay on Private Judgment take up how Christian doctrine grows and on what authority belief rests. The notes Newman added in 1871 set his later judgment beside his earlier argument. The volume records the period in which, by his own account, his Anglican position gave way, and it is read both as Anglican apologetic and as a stage on the road to the Essay on Development.

This is No. 40 of Lérins Newman, the second volume of Essays Critical and Historical within its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. Newman’s text is set from the 1871 edition, keeping the dates of first publication at the head of each essay. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the essays and the years 1840 to 1846, and explanatory notes on the authors, controversies and historical figures they discuss. Newman’s own notes, including those he wrote as a Catholic, stand as he left them, and the Postscript closes the volume as he placed it.

title: Tracts Theological and Ecclesiastical
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s technical studies of the early Church, from Latin dissertations on Athanasius written in Rome in 1847 to the causes of Arianism, the Ignatian letters, Cyril’s formula and the Douay Bible.
description: Tracts Theological and Ecclesiastical gathers seven studies written by John Henry Newman over more than forty years, in a volume whose Advertisement is dated from Birmingham on 5 January 1874. It opens with four Latin dissertations, among them one on the fourth Oration of St. Athanasius against the Arians and two on the anathemas of Nicaea, dedicated to Antonio Bresciani, Rector of the Collegio Urbano in Rome. Then come an essay on the text of the seven Epistles of St. Ignatius, begun in notes of 1828 and completed in 1870, a long study of the causes of the rise and successes of Arianism, the Heresy of Apollinaris from notes of 1835, and St. Cyril’s formula from the Atlantis of 1858. The volume closes with the Ordo de Tempore in the Roman Breviary and the history of the text of the Rheims and Douay Bible.

Much of the book is close scholarship on texts and terms. The Ignatius essay defends the substantial genuineness of the seven letters against the case built on the shorter Syriac text that William Cureton published in 1845. The study of Arianism traces the tradition of the doctrine of the Holy Trinity before Nicaea, and the openings that early ways of speaking, such as the principatus of the Father and the temporal gennesis of the Son, gave to heresy. The Apollinaris and Cyril essays turn to the doctrine of the Incarnation. The volume shows the patristic learning behind Newman’s better known books, from The Arians of the Fourth Century to the Essay on Development, and its later pieces apply that learning to the Catholic liturgy and the English Catholic Bible.

This is No. 41 of Lérins Newman, part of its collected essays, sketches and verse. The text is set from the 1874 collection, with Newman’s Advertisement, his list of the editions of the Fathers he used, and his corrigenda. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction that sets each tract in its time and controversy, and explanatory notes that identify the Fathers, councils and modern critics Newman cites and gloss the Greek and Latin terms on which his arguments turn. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them, in the languages he wrote them in.

title: Discussions and Arguments on Various Subjects
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Six pieces from 1836 to 1866, among them Newman’s Tract lectures on Antichrist and on Scripture and the Creed, and his letters to the Times answering Sir Robert Peel on the Tamworth Reading Room.
description: Discussions and Arguments on Various Subjects is a volume John Henry Newman issued in January 1872 toward the uniform edition of his works, dedicated to his old Oxford friend Henry Arthur Woodgate. It holds six pieces. How to Accomplish It is a discussion between two Anglicans, first printed in the British Magazine in 1836 as Home Thoughts Abroad. The Patristical Idea of Antichrist and Holy Scripture in its Relation to the Catholic Creed are Tracts 83 and 85, published in 1838. The Tamworth Reading Room appeared in the Times in February 1841 over the name Catholicus. Who’s to Blame? is a set of letters written in the spring of 1855 for the Catholic Standard. An Internal Argument for Christianity is a review from the Month of June 1866.

The Tamworth Reading Room is the best known piece. Peel, opening a library and reading room at Tamworth, had spoken as if secular knowledge could make men morally better and bind society together. Newman answers in seven letters, whose headings carry the argument. Secular knowledge, they say, is not the principle, the means or the antecedent of moral improvement, nor a principle of social unity or of action, and without personal religion it tends to unbelief. The lectures on Scripture and the Creed compare the difficulties of proving the Creed from Scripture with the difficulties of the canon itself. Who’s to Blame? studies the British constitution at a time of national strain by setting the character of Englishmen beside that of the Athenians.

This is No. 42 of Lérins Newman, within its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. Newman’s text is set from the 1872 edition, with his Advertisement on the origin of each piece. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction to the six pieces and their occasions, from the Tracts for the Times to the Crimean War and the Catholic press of the 1860s, and explanatory notes on the persons, books and public events Newman answers. Newman’s own notes stand as he left them, including the brackets he added when he reprinted the pieces.

title: Historical Sketches, Volume 1
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s lectures of 1853 on the history of the Turks, given as Russia and Turkey moved toward war, with his early encyclopedia articles on Cicero and Apollonius of Tyana and his Anglican papers on primitive Christianity.
description: Historical Sketches, Volume 1, is the first of three volumes in which John Henry Newman gathered his historical writing in 1872, dedicated on 23 October of that year to David Moriarty, Bishop of Kerry. Most of it is taken up by nine lectures on the history of the Turks in its relation to Christianity, given in 1853 when the collision between Russia and Turkey was, as the first lecture says, engaging public attention. They run from the tribes of the north and the Tartars, through the Turk and the Saracen and the Pope and the Turk, to the past, present and future of the Ottomans. Then come two articles written for the Encyclopaedia Metropolitana, on Marcus Tullius Cicero and on Apollonius of Tyana, and five chapters on primitive Christianity that ask what St. Ambrose, Vincent of Lerins and the Apostolical Canons say.

The Turkish lectures weigh barbarism against civilization and ask what the past of the Ottomans implied for their future, with chronological tables for the general reader. The encyclopedia articles are among Newman’s earliest published prose. The life of Cicero follows the orator through Roman politics, and the piece on Apollonius argues against the attempt, made in the early centuries and revived in England, to set the Pythagorean wonder-worker up as a rival to Christ. The papers on primitive Christianity, which the dedication calls the work of an Anglican controversialist, use the lives of Ambrose and his contemporaries to show the Church of the fourth century in practice. Together they show the range of Newman’s historical reading across three decades.

This is No. 43 of Lérins Newman, the first of the three volumes of Historical Sketches in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. The text is set from the 1872 collection, with the notes and chronological tables of the Turkish lectures. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the three groups of writings and their dates, and explanatory notes on the peoples, rulers and places that a modern reader may not know. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them, including the classical references of the Cicero and Apollonius articles.

title: Historical Sketches, Volume 2
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Portraits of the Fathers drawn from their own letters and lives, Basil and Gregory, Antony, Augustine, Martin, Chrysostom and Theodoret, with Newman’s two essays on St. Benedict and the Benedictine schools.
description: Historical Sketches, Volume 2, gathers John Henry Newman’s studies of the early and early medieval Church. The largest part is The Church of the Fathers, papers which, as the Advertisement says, appeared with two or three exceptions in the British Magazine from 1833, and which were dedicated to Isaac Williams in February 1840. Its chapters treat the trials and labours of Basil, Basil and Gregory, the rise and fall of Gregory, Antony in conflict and in calm, Augustine and the Vandals, the Conversion of Augustine, Demetrias, and Martin and Maximus. The volume adds St. Chrysostom, from the Rambler of 1859, the Trials of Theodoret, and two essays from the Atlantis of 1858 and 1859, The Mission of St. Benedict and The Benedictine Schools.

Newman’s aim in The Church of the Fathers was to show the tone, habits and manners of the early Church through its saints, often in their own words, which he translated at length. The Conversion of Augustine retells the scene in the garden at Milan from the Confessions. The St. Chrysostom chapters follow the bishop from Constantinople to exile and death, and the Theodoret study traces the Bishop of Cyrrhus from his monastic youth through the Council of Ephesus to his last years. The Benedictine essays, written for the Catholic University’s journal, describe the monks as patient restorers of land and learning after the fall of Rome. The papers come partly from Newman’s Anglican years and partly from his Catholic ones, and here the two sit side by side.

This is No. 44 of Lérins Newman, the second volume of Historical Sketches in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. Newman’s text is set from the 1872 collection, with the dedication to Isaac Williams, the Advertisement and the chronology of contemporary events. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the papers and their first readers, and explanatory notes on the saints, places and ancient sources Newman draws on. His own notes and translations stand as he left them, and the order of the papers is his.

title: Historical Sketches, Volume 3
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s sketch of what a university is and how universities grew, written in Dublin in 1854, with his essays on the Northmen and Normans, on medieval Oxford and on the Convocation of Canterbury.
description: Historical Sketches, Volume 3, opens with The Rise and Progress of Universities, twenty chapters that first appeared in 1854 in the Dublin Catholic University Gazette, while John Henry Newman was Rector of the new Catholic University of Ireland. They were published in 1856 as Office and Work of Universities, dedicated from Dublin to James Hope Scott, and given their present title in 1872. The chapters run from What is a University? and the site of a university to student life at Athens, the Sophists, the Lombards, the isles of the north, the schools of Charlemagne, the schoolmen, Abelard, and the colleges of Oxford. The volume adds The Northmen and Normans in England and Ireland from the Rambler of 1859, Medieval Oxford from the British Critic of 1838, and five chapters on the Convocation of Canterbury.

The university chapters are lighter in manner than the Dublin discourses that became The Idea of a University. Newman wrote them, as the Advertisement says, under a profession of incognito and in a conversational tone, and kept both when he reprinted them. Their recurring point is that a university lives by the personal influence of teachers on students, and that colleges are the corrective that discipline a university’s breadth. He draws it from Athens, from the medieval schools and from Oxford, which he knew from within. The Northmen essay treats the Danes and Normans in the history of the Church in England and Ireland. The Convocation chapters examine the constitution of the ancient synod of the province of Canterbury, its two houses, and its relation to the Crown.

This is No. 45 of Lérins Newman, and the last of the three volumes of Historical Sketches in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. The text is set from the 1872 collection, with Newman’s dedication of 1856 and his Advertisement. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the Dublin university and on the other papers gathered here, and explanatory notes on the scholars, schools and institutions Newman names. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them, and the bracketed notes of first publication stand at the head of the later papers.

title: Sayings of Cardinal Newman
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Short speeches and sermons from Newman’s Catholic life, from a Birmingham lecture on poetry in 1849 to his last reply to an address in July 1890, many of them as the newspapers reported them.
description: Sayings of Cardinal Newman, gathered in 1890, is a collection of speeches and sermons that John Henry Newman delivered on occasions of interest during his Catholic life. It begins with a lecture on the characteristics of poetry given at St. Chad’s Schools, Birmingham, in 1849, and ends with his reply to the Catholic Truth Society at its Birmingham conference in July 1890, headed For the last Time. Between them come remarks on receiving converts from Anglicanism, on leaving the rectorship of the Catholic University of Ireland, on writing the Apologia, at the funeral of Henry Wilberforce, and on his elevation to the Sacred College. There are words to the boys of the Oratory School, the sermons of In an Oxford Pulpit again, and his reply on Mr. Ouless’s portrait of him.

Most of the occasions are public and modest, an address from a parish, a school prize day, a visit from a society, and Newman’s answers are brief. Read together, they show the old Cardinal thanking his well-wishers and speaking of the relations between Catholics and Protestants in England, of the need of discipline, and of the conversion of England. The Oxford sermons were preached at St. Aloysius on 23 May 1880, while he was the guest of Trinity College, which had made him an Honorary Fellow two years before. They were the first he had preached in any Oxford pulpit since he left the Church of England. The book is less a work than a record, and its use is in showing how Newman spoke when he was not writing.

This is No. 46 of Lérins Newman, in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. The book holds Newman’s words at one remove. Some pieces give his replies in the first person, as he spoke or wrote them. Many others are reports of his speeches and sermons in the third person, written by those who heard them, and the short accounts of each occasion are the reporters’ and the compiler’s. The text is set from the 1890 collection. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the occasions and the reporting behind them, and explanatory notes on people, places and events. Any notes in the original are kept as they were left.

title: Addresses to Cardinal Newman with His Replies
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The addresses that reached Newman from colleges, chapters, societies and whole countries when Leo XIII made him a Cardinal in 1879, with his replies, among them the Biglietto Speech against liberalism in religion.
description: Addresses to Cardinal Newman with His Replies collects the congratulations sent to John Henry Newman from 1879 to 1881, after Pope Leo XIII raised him to the Sacred College, together with what he said or wrote in answer. It was prepared by Father William P. Neville of the Birmingham Oratory, long Newman’s close companion, and printed from his manuscript after Neville’s death, with an Advertisement dated 17 July 1905. Neville’s Prefatory Narrative introduces the replies. The addresses come from the Jesuits of St. Beuno’s, the Benedictines of Downside, the chapters of Birmingham and Westminster, Trinity College, Oxford, the Catholic University of Ireland, and from Ireland, Australia and the United States. The book also records the Biglietto Speech, given at the Palazzo della Pigna in Rome on 12 May 1879.

The Biglietto Speech is the chief piece, and the one most often quoted. Receiving the notice of his elevation, Newman said that for thirty, forty, fifty years he had resisted to the best of his powers “the spirit of liberalism in religion.” He defined it as the doctrine that there is no positive truth in religion, and that one creed is as good as another. The replies that follow are shorter and more personal. He speaks to schoolboys and seminarians, to the Catholic Union and the Catholic Young Men’s Societies, to the clergy of Lancashire and to the people of the Oratory mission. Together they show how Newman understood the honour, and what he chose to say about his life’s work near its end.

This is No. 47 of Lérins Newman, the last title in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. Most of the words in the book are other people’s. The addresses are the work of the bodies that sent them, and the narrative that links them is Neville’s. Newman’s part is his replies, spoken or written, the Biglietto Speech among them. The text is set from Neville’s 1905 volume, with its appendix of letters. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the cardinalate and the making of the book, and explanatory notes on the senders and occasions. Neville’s notes and Newman’s are kept as they were left.

title: Heretics · Orthodoxy
author: G. K. Chesterton
lead: G. K. Chesterton’s two books of argument with the modern world, Heretics (1905), on the leading writers and ideas of his day, and Orthodoxy (1908), his account of how he came to believe the Christian faith, in one volume.
description: Heretics was published by John Lane at the Bodley Head in 1905, when Chesterton was in his early thirties and writing regularly for the London press. Its twenty chapters, opening and closing with remarks “on the Importance of Orthodoxy”, take up Rudyard Kipling, George Bernard Shaw, H. G. Wells, George Moore, Whistler and others, with essays on the yellow press, the aesthetes, the Celtic revival, the family and the novelists of the slums. The book drew a challenge. The critic G. S. Street wrote that he would begin to worry about his own philosophy when Chesterton had given his. Chesterton answered with Orthodoxy, published by John Lane in 1908, whose preface calls it a companion to Heretics, meant to put the positive side beside the negative and therefore unavoidably autobiographical. Its nine chapters run from “Introduction in Defence of Everything Else” through “The Suicide of Thought”, “The Ethics of Elfland” and “The Paradoxes of Christianity” to “Authority and the Adventurer”.

In Heretics Chesterton complains less that his contemporaries hold wrong opinions than that they have ceased to think that opinions about ultimate things matter. Against them he sets the older view, that “the most practical and important thing about a man is still his view of the universe.” In Orthodoxy he gives his own. He pictures himself as an English yachtsman who “slightly miscalculated his course and discovered England under the impression that it was a new island in the South Seas”: he had set out to find a philosophy of his own and found that he had arrived at the old one. The chapters pass through the madness of pure logic, the moral sense learned from fairy tales and the balance of opposites he finds in Christian teaching. He keeps to the theology “sufficiently summarized in the Apostles’ Creed,” and sets aside the question of where authority to proclaim it now lies. He was then a member of the Church of England, and he was received into the Catholic Church in 1922. The two books have been read together since, by Christians of many churches as a defence of the belief they hold in common, and by others as an argument to be answered.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the writers, politicians, philosophers and controversies Chesterton names, from Kipling, Shaw and Wells to Nietzsche, Tolstoy and the New Theology of R. J. Campbell.

title: The Everlasting Man · The Thing
author: G. K. Chesterton
lead: G. K. Chesterton’s two books of his Catholic years, The Everlasting Man (1925), his outline of human and Christian history, and The Thing (1929), his essays in defence of the Catholic faith, in one volume.
description: The Everlasting Man was published by Hodder and Stoughton in London in 1925, three years after Chesterton was received into the Catholic Church. Its prefatory note salutes H. G. Wells, and the book is commonly read as an answer to Wells’s Outline of History of 1919–20. After an introduction come two parts, “On the Creature Called Man”, from “The Man in the Cave” to “The End of the World”, and “On the Man Called Christ”, from “The God in the Cave” to “The Five Deaths of the Faith”, with two appendices. The Thing was published by Sheed and Ward in London in 1929, and in New York by Dodd, Mead in 1930 as The Thing: Why I Am a Catholic. It gathers an introduction and thirty-four papers, written as Chesterton’s part in the religious controversy then carried on in the press, among them “Is Humanism a Religion?”, “The Drift from Domesticity” and “Why I Am a Catholic”.

In The Everlasting Man Chesterton argues that man, seen plainly, is a strange creature, the only one that drew pictures on the walls of caves, and that the story of Christ and the Church cannot be fitted into a scheme of comparative religion. He sets the cave at Bethlehem beside the cave where man first painted, and he traces how the faith has seemed to die five times and has each time returned. C. S. Lewis wrote in Surprised by Joy (1955) that reading it while he was still an atheist first showed him a Christian account of history that made sense to him. Others have found its prehistory overtaken by later scholarship. The Thing takes its title from Chesterton’s name for the Catholic faith itself, a definite thing to be accepted or refused. Its essays answer the Protestant, modernist and humanist critics of the day, among them Dean Inge and Bishop Barnes, and “The Drift from Domesticity” sets out the principle of the fence across a road, since widely cited as “Chesterton’s fence”. Protestant readers have contested many of its judgements on the Reformation.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the peoples, religions, philosophers, churchmen and controversies Chesterton names, from the cave painters, Plato and Arius to Darwin, Wells, Dean Inge and Bishop Barnes.

title: What’s Wrong with the World · The Outline of Sanity
author: G. K. Chesterton
lead: G. K. Chesterton’s two books on the home and small property, What’s Wrong with the World (1910), his case for the family against the reformers of his day, and The Outline of Sanity (1926), his case for the wide distribution of property, in one volume.
description: What’s Wrong with the World was published by Cassell in London in 1910, with a dedication to his friend the Liberal politician C. F. G. Masterman. Its five parts are “The Homelessness of Man”, “Imperialism, or the Mistake about Man”, “Feminism, or the Mistake about Woman”, “Education, or the Mistake about the Child” and “The Home of Man”, followed by three notes, the last of them on peasant proprietorship. The Outline of Sanity was published by Methuen in London in 1926, gathered from notes in his own paper, G.K.’s Weekly, founded the year before. Its six parts treat general ideas, big business, the land, machinery and emigration, and end in a summary. Its title echoes Wells’s Outline of History, and it appeared in the year the Distributist League was founded, with Chesterton as its president.

The first book states the problem. Chesterton argues that reformers dispute about remedies without agreeing on what health would be, and his own ideal is the free family in its own home, which he holds modern economic life has taken from the poor. His parable of Hudge and Gudge, the reformer who builds tenements and the plutocrat who defends the slums, suggests that the two quarrel in public and serve one another in private. His positions on women and on education were contested in his own day and since. The second book gives his remedy: not a new system but property in the hands of as many people as possible, the small shop, the family farm and the craftsman’s workshop, against both the trusts and socialism. The cause he and Hilaire Belloc called distributism drew on Leo XIII’s encyclical Rerum Novarum (1891). It has found readers since among Catholic social thinkers and others concerned with small property and local economies, and critics who judge it impractical.

No. 3 of Lérins Chesterton will print What’s Wrong with the World in the text of 1910, with the dedication and the three notes, and The Outline of Sanity in the text of the London first edition of 1926. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the politicians, reformers, economists and movements Chesterton names, from the Liberal and Tory parties of 1910 and the suffragettes to the trusts, the big shops and Henry Ford.

title: Tremendous Trifles · All Things Considered
author: G. K. Chesterton
lead: Two complete books of G. K. Chesterton’s short essays from the Daily News, Tremendous Trifles (1909) and All Things Considered (1908), in one volume.
description: In the first decade of the century Chesterton wrote a weekly column for the Daily News, and Methuen gathered the papers into books. Tremendous Trifles (1909) holds thirty-nine of them, among them “A Piece of Chalk”, “The Twelve Men”, written after he had served on a jury, “What I Found in My Pocket”, “The Dragon’s Grandmother”, “The Red Angel”, “The Toy Theatre” and “The Shop of Ghosts”. Its preface calls the sketches “a sort of sporadic diary”, kept in public “for bread and cheese”. All Things Considered (1908) holds thirty-five more, from “The Case for the Ephemeral” and “Cockneys and Their Jokes” to “The Fallacy of Success”, “On Running After One’s Hat”, “Science and Religion”, “Fairy Tales”, “The Maid of Orleans” and “Christmas”.

The essays take some small thing, a hat blown off in the wind, a piece of chalk, the contents of a pocket, a jury box, and find in it a question about the world. The preface to Tremendous Trifles puts the method plainly: the reader’s eye, straying from the page, is a thousand to one resting on something he has never truly seen, and the essays ask him to look again. “The Fallacy of Success” mocks the books that promise to teach the secret of getting on, and “The Red Angel” defends fairy tales against those who would keep them from children. The essays were written in the same years as Heretics and Orthodoxy, and many of them have been reprinted in later collections of his essays.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the people, places, papers and controversies of Edwardian England that the essays name, from the Zola affair and the Captain of Köpenick to Joan of Arc, Fielding’s Tom Jones and Dickens.

title: Phantastes · Lilith
author: George MacDonald
lead: George MacDonald’s first and last romances for grown readers, Phantastes (1858) and Lilith (1895), in one volume.
description: MacDonald had given up his only pastorate, at Arundel in Sussex, and was living by writing and lecturing when Smith, Elder and Co. published Phantastes in London in 1858, with the subtitle A Faerie Romance for Men and Women. Its twenty-five chapters are each headed by lines from poets and writers, among them Shelley, Novalis, Goethe, Spenser and Chaucer. In 1905 his son Greville MacDonald issued a new edition with illustrations by Arthur Hughes. Lilith came thirty-seven years later. Chatto and Windus published it in London in 1895, and Dodd, Mead the same year in New York, when MacDonald was seventy and had worked on it through several drafts. It has forty-seven chapters and opens with a passage from Thoreau’s essay Walking. Its title figure comes from Jewish legend, in which Lilith is the first wife of Adam.

In Phantastes the young Anodos wakes on the morning after his twenty-first birthday to find the basin in his room overflowing into a stream and the carpet turning to grass. In the forest beyond he meets the spirits of the trees, takes on in the cottage of an ogress a dark shadow that will not leave him, and goes in search of a white lady he once sang out of her sleep in marble. In Lilith Mr Vane follows the old librarian of his house, who also goes about as a raven, through a mirror into a country that lies alongside our own, refuses a couch among the sleepers in a great chamber of the dead, and comes at last to the city of Bulika and its princess. MacDonald gives neither book a key. C. S. Lewis bought Phantastes at Leatherhead station in 1916 and wrote in Surprised by Joy of that reading as the moment his imagination was changed. Readers have long differed over Lilith, some finding in it MacDonald’s hope for the restoration of all at its plainest, others a vision that leaves the question open. W. H. Auden introduced the two books together in an American edition of 1954.

No. 1 of Lérins MacDonald prints Phantastes in the text of the 1905 edition, with Greville MacDonald’s preface, and Lilith in the text of 1895. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the poets and writers MacDonald quotes, from Novalis, Shelley and Spenser to Thoreau, on the Jewish legends of Lilith, Adam and Eve, and on the books’ allusions to Scripture.

title: Unspoken Sermons
author: George MacDonald
lead: George MacDonald’s three series of Unspoken Sermons, published in 1867, 1885 and 1889, complete in one volume.
description: MacDonald trained for the Congregational ministry at Highbury College in London and held one pastorate, at Arundel in Sussex, which he gave up in 1853 after objections to his teaching. In 1867 Alexander Strahan published the first volume of the sermons he wrote for the page, under the Greek words Epea Aptera, ‘wingless words’, offered first to his wife as sermons “gathered and rubbed in my hands upon broken Sabbaths.” Longmans, Green and Co. published the second series in 1885, its dedication dated from the family’s house at Bordighera on the Italian Riviera, and the third in 1889. Each series holds twelve sermons, thirty-six in all, from The Child in the Midst and The Consuming Fire through The Way, The Last Farthing and Abba, Father! to The Creation in Christ, Justice and The Inheritance.

Each sermon takes a verse, most often a saying of Jesus, and presses on it. The Consuming Fire reads Hebrews 12:29 as the love of God that will burn away all that is not good in those it loves, and opens with the sentence “Nothing is inexorable but love.” The Last Farthing reads the debtor’s prison as a punishment that purifies and has an end. Justice, the longest of all, asks why God is bound to punish sin, and answers that God’s justice is set on making the sinner right, rejecting any account of the atonement in which the suffering of the innocent satisfies justice for the guilty. Readers have divided over the sermons since they appeared. Some take MacDonald for a Christian universalist, others for a writer of hope who stops short of a doctrine, and many Reformed and evangelical readers have answered Justice as a denial of penal substitution. C. S. Lewis drew many of the readings in his George MacDonald: An Anthology (1946) from these sermons, and made MacDonald the narrator’s guide in The Great Divorce.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the Scripture each sermon takes up, the Greek words MacDonald weighs, and the writers and debates on judgement and the atonement in which the sermons have been read.
subtitle: First, Second and Third Series

title: At the Back of the North Wind · Dealings with the Fairies
author: George MacDonald
lead: George MacDonald’s fairy tales for children, At the Back of the North Wind (1871) and the five tales of Dealings with the Fairies (1867), in one volume.
description: Alexander Strahan published Dealings with the Fairies in London in 1867, a small volume illustrated by MacDonald’s friend the painter Arthur Hughes. It gathers five tales: The Light Princess, The Giant’s Heart, The Shadows, Cross Purposes and The Golden Key. The Light Princess and The Shadows had first been told within MacDonald’s novel Adela Cathcart (1864), and The Golden Key appeared here for the first time. At the Back of the North Wind first ran as a serial in Good Words for the Young, a monthly for children, from 1868 to 1870, and MacDonald became the magazine’s editor while it was running. Strahan and Co. issued it as a book in 1871, with wood engravings by the brothers Dalziel after drawings by Hughes. Its thirty-eight chapters move between a hay-loft over a London coach-house, the streets and cab-ranks of the city, the seaside, and the country at the back of the north wind itself.

Diamond, named after the horse that sleeps in the stall beneath his bed, is woken one night by the North Wind blowing through a hole in the boards. She comes to him as a tall and beautiful woman or as something small enough to hide behind a primrose, and carries him out over the city by night. Some of her errands he cannot understand, for she sinks ships as well as sweeping the streets clean, and her answers to his questions stand at the centre of the book, which has been read both as a story for children and as a meditation on suffering and death. In the earlier tales a princess robbed of her gravity floats through the palace laughing at everything, two children find where a cruel giant has hidden his heart, and in The Golden Key a boy and a girl, Mossy and Tangle, set out for the country from which the shadows fall. In 1964 J. R. R. Tolkien agreed to write a preface for a new edition of The Golden Key, and what he began became his story Smith of Wootton Major.

title: The Princess and the Goblin · The Princess and Curdie
author: George MacDonald
lead: George MacDonald’s two books of the Princess Irene and the miner’s son Curdie, The Princess and the Goblin (1872) and its sequel The Princess and Curdie (1883), in one volume.
description: The Princess and the Goblin ran as a serial in Good Words for the Young, the children’s monthly MacDonald then edited, from November 1870 to June 1871, and Strahan and Co. published it as a book in 1872 with illustrations by Arthur Hughes. It has thirty-two chapters. MacDonald returned to its people in The Princess and Curdie, which ran from January to June 1877 in Good Things for the Young of All Ages, the monthly that Good Words for the Young had become, and waited five years for a book. Chatto and Windus published it in London with illustrations by James Allen, issued for Christmas 1882 with the date 1883 on its title page. It has thirty-five chapters.

Irene, a king’s daughter of about eight, is being brought up in a house half castle and half farmhouse on a mountainside. Under the mountain live the goblins, a people who went underground long ago and grew misshapen and spiteful there, and who cannot bear to hear a rhyme. Lost one rainy day on an unfamiliar stair, Irene finds at the top of the house an old and beautiful lady who says she is her great-great-grandmother and who sits spinning a thread too fine to see, while Curdie, a miner’s son of about twelve, overhears the goblins plotting in the dark of the mines. In the sequel the old princess plunges Curdie’s hands into a fire of burning roses, so that by taking any hand in his own he can tell whether its owner is growing into a beast, and sends him with the strange creature Lina to the royal city of Gwyntystorm, where the king lies sick among courtiers who are not what they seem. The second book is darker than the first and turns on the judgement of a city. G. K. Chesterton wrote in 1924 that The Princess and the Goblin had made a difference to his whole existence, and J. R. R. Tolkien acknowledged in a letter that the orcs of his own stories owed a good deal to MacDonald’s goblins.

title: The Commonitory
author: Vincent of Lérins
lead: Vincent of Lérins’s rule for telling the Catholic faith from heresy, by holding to what has been believed everywhere, always and by all, written by a monk of Lérins about 434.
description: Vincent was a monk and presbyter of the monastery on Lérins, the island off the coast of Provence where Honoratus had founded a community early in the fifth century. He wrote the Commonitory, a word he glosses as “an aid to memory,” under the name Peregrinus, and he refers to the council held at Ephesus some three years before, which dates the work to about 434. Of the two Commonitories he wrote, the second was lost early, and the book as it survives closes with Vincent’s own summary of both. Its thirty-three chapters set out a method for a Christian faced with rival teachers who all appeal to Scripture, from Novatian, Sabellius and Arius to Pelagius and Nestorius. Vincent draws his instances from the African dispute over rebaptism, the Arian crisis and the Council of Ephesus, and among his warning examples are Origen and Tertullian, whom he presents as gifted teachers who went astray.

Vincent holds that the faith is guarded in two ways, by the authority of Scripture and by the tradition of the Catholic Church, since Scripture is read in as many senses as it has readers. Within the Church, he writes, “we hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all,” and he tests a doctrine by universality, antiquity and consent. He allows that doctrine grows, as a body grows from childhood to age, so long as it stays the same in kind and is not changed into something else. The book was first printed at Basel in 1528 and was read at once on both sides of the Reformation. Catholic and Anglican writers have appealed to its rule for their claims to the faith of the early Church, the First Vatican Council quoted its chapter on growth in doctrine, and Newman’s Essay on Development weighed the rule against the history. Some readers have taken certain passages as aimed at Augustine’s teaching on grace, a reading others dispute.

No. 1 of Lérins Fathers prints the Commonitory in the translation of C. A. Heurtley, published in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, volume XI, in 1894. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the heretics, councils, bishops and writers Vincent names and on the Scripture he cites. Heurtley’s notes are kept.

title: The Apostolic Fathers
subtitle: Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, the Didache, Barnabas, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Epistle to Diognetus, Papias and Quadratus
lead: The earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament, letters, a homily, a church order, a book of visions and an apology from the end of the first century and the second, gathered under the name of the Apostolic Fathers.
description: The name was given in the seventeenth century to writers thought to have known the apostles or their followers. It opens with the letter of the church of Rome to the church of Corinth, known as First Clement and written about 96, when a party at Corinth had removed its presbyters. Second Clement is an ancient homily. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote his seven letters early in the second century, to churches of Asia, to Rome and to Polycarp, while he was taken under guard to his death at Rome. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, wrote to the Philippians, and the Martyrdom of Polycarp is his church’s account of his death. The Didache, a short church order, was found in 1873 by Philotheos Bryennios in a manuscript at Constantinople and published ten years later. The Epistle of Barnabas, the Shepherd of Hermas in its Visions, Mandates and Similitudes, the Epistle to Diognetus, the fragments of Papias of Hierapolis with the sayings of the elders preserved in Irenaeus, and the fragment of the apology Quadratus addressed to Hadrian complete the book.

The writings show the churches in the generations after the apostles. Clement writes of the order the apostles left for the appointment of presbyters, Ignatius of one bishop with his presbyters and deacons and of one Eucharist, and the Didache gives prayers for the Eucharist, a rule for baptism and the teaching of the Two Ways. Hermas treats repentance after baptism, and the letter to Diognetus explains the Christians to an inquirer. The letters of Ignatius became a point of contest after the Reformation. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican writers cited them for the episcopate and the Eucharist, while Presbyterian and other Protestant scholars questioned their genuineness or their witness to church order, until the work of James Ussher in the seventeenth century and of Lightfoot in the nineteenth persuaded most scholars that the seven letters of the middle recension are genuine.

McGiffert’s translation of Eusebius’s Church History. title: The First and Second Apologies of St. Justin Martyr
author: St. Justin Martyr
lead: Two defences of the Christians addressed to the Roman authorities by Justin, a philosopher who became a Christian, taught at Rome and died there as a martyr, written in the middle of the second century.
description: Justin was born at Flavia Neapolis in Samaria and came to the faith, by his own account, after trying the schools of the philosophers. He taught at Rome and was put to death there with several companions about 165, under the prefect Rusticus. The First Apology, written about 155, is addressed to the emperor Antoninus Pius, to his son Verissimus, later the emperor Marcus Aurelius, to Lucius, and to the senate and people of Rome. It closes with the rescript of Hadrian to Minucius Fundanus on the trial of Christians. The Second Apology, addressed to the Roman senate, was prompted by the execution of Ptolemaeus and two others under Urbicus, prefect of the city, for confessing that they were Christians.

Justin asks that Christians be judged by what they do, not condemned for the name, and he answers the charges of atheism and immorality. He argues from the fulfilment of the Hebrew prophets in Christ, and he teaches that Christ is the Word in whom the whole human race shares, so that “there seem to be seeds of truth among all men.” In its closing chapters the First Apology describes baptism, the Eucharist and the Sunday assembly of the church at Rome, the fullest account of Christian worship to survive from the second century. Of the bread and the cup Justin writes, “not as common bread and common drink do we receive these.” These chapters are read by historians of the liturgy in every tradition. Catholic and Orthodox writers cite them for the Eucharist as the flesh and blood of Christ, Protestant writers have weighed them in their own debates over the sacrament, and his teaching on the Word has been taken up by those who ask how the Gospel stands to Greek philosophy.

title: The Church History of Eusebius
author: Eusebius of Caesarea
lead: The first history of the Christian Church, from the coming of Christ to the victory of Constantine, written in ten books by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, and completed about 325.
description: Eusebius was born about 260 and studied at Caesarea under the presbyter Pamphilus, who died a martyr in the persecution under Diocletian, and he worked in the library that Origen and Pamphilus had gathered there. He became bishop of Caesarea about 313 and took part in the Council of Nicaea in 325. He wrote the Church History over many years and issued it in more than one edition, the last after Constantine’s defeat of Licinius in 324. In the first book he names his subjects: the successions of the apostles, the chief events of the Church’s history, its teachers and writers, the heretics, the fate of the Jews, and the martyrs. Books 2 to 7 run from the apostles to his own day. Books 8 to 10 tell of the Great Persecution, which Eusebius lived through, and of the peace that followed under Constantine.

Eusebius builds his history from documents and quotes them at length: Hegesippus, Papias, Dionysius of Corinth, Irenaeus, the letter of the churches of Lyons and Vienne on their martyrs, and many letters of bishops. Much of this survives only in his pages. He gives lists of the bishops of Rome, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem, and his account of the books of the New Testament divides them into those acknowledged, those disputed and those rejected. Rufinus put the History into Latin and carried it on, and Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret continued it in Greek. Historians of every tradition have depended on it for the first three centuries. Catholic and Orthodox writers have drawn on its lists of bishops and its witness to the apostolic churches, Protestant writers on its account of the canon and its record of the martyrs, and modern scholars have debated how far his judgments can be trusted and how far his own part in the Arian controversy shaped his work.

title: On the Incarnation of the Word
author: St. Athanasius
lead: Athanasius of Alexandria’s account of why the Word of God took a human body, died and rose again, written in the first half of the fourth century as the second part of a two-book defence of the faith.
description: Athanasius was born about 296, attended the Council of Nicaea in 325 as a deacon of Bishop Alexander, and was bishop of Alexandria from 328 until his death in 373, a tenure broken by five exiles. On the Incarnation is the second half of a work whose first part, Against the Heathen, answers the worship of idols. Both are addressed to a Christian reader who had asked for an account of the faith. The date is disputed. Some scholars place the pair about 318, before Arius’s teaching became a public controversy, since neither names him, and others in the middle 330s. The book runs in fifty-seven short chapters. Its argument moves from creation and the fall to the death and resurrection of the Word, then to the signs of his victory in the world, and closes with answers to Jewish and Greek objectors.

Athanasius begins from creation. Humankind was made through the Word in the image of God, fell by transgression into corruption and death, and could be restored only by the Word through whom it was first made. The Word therefore took a body from the Virgin, gave it up to death on behalf of all, and raised it incorruptible, so that death lost its hold on those who belong to him. “For He was made man that we might be made God,” Athanasius writes near the end. That sentence has stood at the centre of Orthodox teaching on deification, and Eastern writers have read the whole book in its light. Catholic and Protestant readers have read it as an early account of the Incarnation and of Christ’s death for all, and its answers to pagan and Jewish objections have been studied as an example of Christian apologetic in the age of Constantine.

title: The Catechetical Lectures of St. Cyril of Jerusalem
author: St. Cyril of Jerusalem
lead: The instructions Cyril of Jerusalem gave to candidates for baptism in Lent and to the newly baptized at Easter, delivered in the church Constantine had built over the place of Christ’s death and burial, about 350.
description: Cyril was bishop of Jerusalem from about 350 until his death in 386, and he was driven into exile three times in the disputes that followed Nicaea. The lectures were spoken, not written, and were taken down by a hearer. A Procatechesis, or introductory lecture, is followed by eighteen Catechetical Lectures, given in Lent to those preparing for baptism at Easter. They treat sin, repentance, baptism and faith, and then go through the creed of the church of Jerusalem article by article. Five Mystagogic Lectures, given in Easter week to the newly baptized, explain the rites they had just received: the renunciation of Satan, baptism, the anointing with chrism, the Eucharist and the liturgy. Some manuscripts give the Mystagogic Lectures to John, Cyril’s successor as bishop, and scholars remain divided on their author.

Cyril asks that every article of the faith be proved from Scripture, for “not even a casual statement must be delivered without the Holy Scriptures.” He treats the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Incarnation, the cross, the resurrection, the Church and the life to come, and he points his hearers to the holy places around them, Golgotha and the tomb among them. The Mystagogic Lectures speak of the bread and wine, after the invocation of the Holy Spirit, as the body and blood of Christ, of the sacrifice offered for the living and the departed, and of the order of the liturgy at Jerusalem in his day. They are among the chief sources for the history of Christian initiation and of the Eucharist. Catholic and Orthodox writers have cited them for the Eucharist and for prayer for the dead, Protestant writers have cited the earlier lectures for the place of Scripture in teaching, and historians of the liturgy in every tradition draw on both.

title: On the Holy Spirit
author: St. Basil the Great
lead: Basil of Caesarea’s defence of the honour due to the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, written for Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, in 375.
description: Basil was bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia from 370 until his death in 379, and with his friend Gregory of Nazianzus and his brother Gregory of Nyssa he is counted among the Cappadocian Fathers. Some of his hearers objected when he gave glory in public prayer to the Father with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit, as well as in the familiar form, to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit. Amphilochius asked him to explain himself, and Basil answered in thirty chapters. He examines the prepositions Scripture uses of the three persons and shows that neither form of the doxology ranks the Son or the Spirit below the Father. He answers the followers of Aetius and Eunomius, who held the Son unlike the Father, and those who denied that the Spirit is to be ranked with the Father and the Son.

Basil teaches that the Spirit is inseparable from the Father and the Son in every work, in creation, in the life of the Church and in the judgment to come, and that he who sanctifies cannot be one of the things sanctified. He gives the Spirit the honour and the worship due to God, though for the sake of peace he holds back from naming him God outright. In the twenty-seventh chapter he distinguishes the teaching set down in Scripture from what the Church has received in unwritten tradition, such as the sign of the cross, turning to the east in prayer and the words of the invocation at the Eucharist. The book prepared the way for the confession of the Spirit at the Council of Constantinople in 381. That chapter has been cited ever since in the debate over Scripture and tradition. Catholic and Orthodox writers appeal to it for the authority of tradition, while Protestant writers have read it as concerning customs of worship rather than doctrine.

title: The Five Theological Orations
author: St. Gregory Nazianzen
lead: Five sermons on the knowledge of God, the divinity of the Son and the divinity of the Holy Spirit, preached at Constantinople by Gregory of Nazianzus in 380.
description: Gregory, son of the bishop of Nazianzus in Cappadocia and friend of Basil from their student days at Athens, was called to Constantinople in 379, when its churches were held by those who rejected the Creed of Nicaea. He gathered a small congregation in a house chapel called the Anastasia, from the Greek word for resurrection, and there in 380 he preached these orations, numbered 27 to 31 among his works. The first asks who may speak of God, when and before whom. The second treats what can be known of God. The third and fourth answer the arguments of the Eunomians against the divinity of the Son, the fourth taking their texts of Scripture one by one. The fifth defends the divinity of the Holy Spirit. In 381 Gregory presided for a time over the Council of Constantinople, then resigned his see and went back to Cappadocia.

Gregory holds that God is beyond the grasp of the mind, that the names Father and Son speak of a relation and not of an essence or an act, and that the Son and the Spirit share one nature with the Father. To those who said that Scripture nowhere calls the Spirit God, he answers that the knowledge of the Trinity was given in stages: the Father openly in the Old Testament, the Son in the New, and the Spirit now dwelling among believers. In the Eastern Church Gregory is called the Theologian, a title he shares with John the Evangelist and Symeon the New Theologian, and it is tied above all to these orations. They have been read by Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant theologians as a statement of the doctrine of the Trinity confessed at Constantinople in 381. His naming of procession as the Spirit’s own property was cited on both sides of the later dispute between East and West over the Filioque.

title: Fifty Spiritual Homilies
author: St. Macarius the Egyptian
lead: Fifty homilies on prayer, grace and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit in the soul, handed down under the name of Macarius the Egyptian, a desert father of the fourth century.
description: Macarius of Egypt, who lived from about 300 to about 390, was a monk of Scetis, the desert west of the Nile Delta, and was remembered as one of the founders of Egyptian monasticism. The fifty homilies have come down in Greek under his name. They are sermons, letters and answers to questions, written for monks and for those who sought their counsel, and several take the form of a dialogue between a teacher and his hearers. Many modern scholars hold that they come not from Egypt but from an unknown author in Syria or Mesopotamia in the later fourth century. Some have connected them with the ascetic movement condemned as Messalian, while others hold that the homilies themselves reject that movement’s errors. The collection of fifty is one of several in which the Macarian writings survive.

The homilies speak of the soul as darkened by the sin that entered with Adam and of the Holy Spirit as the power that cleanses it, dwelling in the heart and bringing the believer to a living knowledge of Christ. They call for constant prayer and watchfulness, and they describe the inner warfare of the soul and its growth as the work of grace together with human effort. The homilies were read widely in Eastern monasticism, and a paraphrase made from them by Symeon Metaphrastes stands in the Philokalia. After the Reformation they found readers among Protestants as well. John Wesley printed extracts from them in the first volume of his Christian Library in 1749, and Pietist writers in Germany drew on them. Orthodox readers have taken them as a witness to the prayer of the heart, and readers in the Pietist and Methodist traditions found in them a teaching on the Spirit’s work in the soul.

title: The Paradise of the Holy Fathers
subtitle: The sayings and lives of the Desert Fathers
lead: The lives and sayings of the monks of the Egyptian desert in the fourth and fifth centuries, as gathered in Syriac in the seventh century and translated into English by E. A. Wallis Budge.
description: The Paradise of the Fathers was compiled in Syriac by Enanisho, a monk of the monastery of Beth Abhe in northern Mesopotamia, at the request of George, Catholicos of the Church of the East, in the second half of the seventh century. He gathered Syriac versions of Greek works on the desert monks. Budge translated the compilation from Syriac manuscripts, first in 1904 and then in a revised form as The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers in 1907. Its first part opens with Athanasius’s Life of Antony, written soon after Antony’s death in 356, and goes on to the Lausiac History of Palladius, written about 420 for Lausus, chamberlain at the court of Constantinople, the rule of the Pachomian monasteries, and the History of the Monks of Egypt ascribed to Jerome. The second part holds the Sayings of the Fathers, the short words and stories of the elders.

The book shows the desert life from the inside: the solitaries of Scetis and Nitria and the communities of Pachomius in Upper Egypt, their fasting, labour, prayer and silence, their struggles with demons and with themselves, and the counsel they gave to those who came to learn. Antony, Macarius, Pambo, Moses the Ethiopian, Evagrius and many others appear in it. The lives and sayings of the desert monks survive in Greek, Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Armenian and Ethiopic collections, and they have been read as guidance for the monastic life in East and West alike. Benedict commends the Lives of the Fathers to his monks, the Orthodox Church keeps the feasts of many of these monks, and in modern times readers outside the monasteries, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, have turned to the sayings.

title: On the Priesthood
author: St. John Chrysostom
lead: John Chrysostom’s dialogue in six books on the dignity and the dangers of the priesthood, written at Antioch before his ordination as priest in 386.
description: John, later called Chrysostom, “golden-mouthed,” was born at Antioch about 347 and studied rhetoric there before he turned to the ascetic life. The work tells of a time when he and his close friend Basil were sought for ordination as bishops. John encouraged Basil to accept, letting him think that he would do the same, and then hid himself, so that Basil was ordained alone. The six books are a dialogue between the two friends, in which John answers Basil’s reproach and explains why he judged himself unfit for so high an office. Scholars differ on the date and on how far the story is history and how far a literary frame, but the work was written before he was ordained priest at Antioch in 386. He became bishop of Constantinople in 398 and died in exile in 407.

John sets the priesthood above every earthly office, because it is given by the Holy Spirit and has charge of souls, and he holds that the priest who stands at the altar and offers the sacrifice must be purer than the monks of the desert, though he lives among people in the world. He writes of ambition and envy among the clergy, the care of widows and virgins, the judgment of the people, the labour of preaching, and the account the priest must give for every soul in his care. The book has been read in East and West as a guide for those entering the ministry and has been put into many languages. Catholic and Orthodox readers have drawn on its teaching on the priest at the altar, and Protestant readers on its chapters on preaching and the care of souls. The liturgy most used in the Orthodox Church bears his name.

title: The City of God
author: St. Augustine
lead: Augustine’s twenty-two books on the city of God and the earthly city, begun after the sack of Rome in 410 and finished about 426.
description: Augustine, bishop of Hippo in North Africa from about 396 until his death in 430, began the City of God in 413, when pagans were blaming the capture of Rome by Alaric and the Goths in 410 on the abandonment of the old gods. He wrote it in parts over some thirteen years and dedicated it to his friend Marcellinus, the imperial commissioner in Africa. In his Retractations he describes its plan. The first ten books answer the pagans: books 1 to 5 those who worship the gods for the sake of this life, and books 6 to 10 those who worship them for the life to come, with a long engagement with the Platonists. The last twelve books set out the origin, the course and the ends of the two cities, the heavenly and the earthly, from the fall of the angels and the creation to the last judgment, the punishment of the wicked and the eternal rest of the saints.

The two cities, Augustine writes, “have been formed by two loves,” the love of self and the love of God, and they are mingled in this world until the judgment separates them. Along the way he treats the Roman past, the philosophers, providence and free will, creation, the fall and original sin, the history of Israel and the prophets, the Church, the resurrection of the body and the vision of God. The book shaped Western thought on history, the Church, peace and the state from the early Middle Ages. Einhard records that Charlemagne had it read to him at meals. Medieval writers drew on it in debates over the powers of popes and kings, the Reformers and their Catholic opponents both appealed to its teaching on grace and the Church, and modern readers of every tradition have taken it up on history and politics.

title: The Conferences of John Cassian
subtitle: On the goal of the monk, on discretion and on prayer
author: St. John Cassian
lead: Four of John Cassian’s conferences with the monks of the Egyptian desert, on the goal of the monastic life, on discretion and on prayer, written at Marseilles in the 420s.
description: Cassian, born about 360, probably in the Roman province of Scythia Minor, entered a monastery at Bethlehem as a young man and then spent years with his friend Germanus among the monks of Egypt. He was later ordained deacon at Constantinople under John Chrysostom, and about 415 he settled at Marseilles, where he founded monasteries for men and for women. There he wrote the Institutes and then the twenty-four Conferences, set out as conversations he and Germanus had held with the elders of the desert. The first ten are dedicated to Leontius, a bishop, and to Helladius, and the next seven to Honoratus, founder of the monastery of Lérins, and to Eucherius, a monk there. This book prints Conferences 1 and 2, with Abba Moses at Scetis, and Conferences 9 and 10, with Abba Isaac.

Abba Moses distinguishes the end of the monk, the kingdom of God, from his immediate goal, purity of heart, to which every fast and vigil is only a means, and in the second conference he names discretion as the virtue that guides all the rest. Abba Isaac describes unceasing prayer as the aim of the whole monastic life and teaches his hearers to keep at all times the verse of the Psalms, “O God, make speed to save me: O Lord, make haste to help me.” Benedict told his monks to read the Conferences, and through his Rule they became part of the reading of Western monasteries. In the East Cassian is honoured as a saint, and the Philokalia includes writings drawn from his works. His thirteenth conference, on grace and free will, not printed here, was criticised by Prosper of Aquitaine, and some later Western writers have called Cassian a Semi-Pelagian, a judgment others have questioned.
