title: St. Patrick
subtitle: His Writings and Muirchu's Life
author: St. Patrick
lead: The two writings of Patrick, the fifth-century bishop in Ireland, his Confession and his Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus, with the hymn known as his Breastplate and the Life of Patrick written by Muirchu in the seventh century.
description: Patrick was a Briton, the son of a deacon and grandson of a priest, who was taken captive to Ireland at about sixteen and kept flocks there for six years before he escaped. He returned to Ireland as a bishop and spent the rest of his life there. His dates are uncertain, and scholars place his mission in the middle or the later part of the fifth century. He wrote the Confession, in Latin, in his old age, to answer those who questioned his mission and to give thanks for his calling. The Letter denounces the soldiers of Coroticus, a British king, who had killed and carried off newly baptized converts. The Breastplate, a hymn of protection in Irish, is ascribed to him by tradition, though most scholars date it later. Muirchu moccu Machtheni wrote his Life of Patrick late in the seventh century at the request of Aed, bishop of Sletty, and the Book of Armagh, written in the early ninth century, preserves both the Life and the Confession.

The Confession tells of Patrick’s captivity and his prayer, the voice in a dream that told him a ship was ready to take him home, the vision in which the Irish called him back, and the labours and dangers of his mission, in a Latin he himself calls unlearned. Muirchu’s Life sets Patrick against the king Loegaire and his druids at Tara, with the paschal fire lit in defiance of the king. Patrick is honoured by the Catholic Church, the Church of Ireland and the Orthodox Church, among others, and his own writings have been read in each for their account of conversion, mission and prayer. Historians distinguish the Patrick of the two letters from the Patrick of the later Lives, and the relation between them, and the claims of Armagh that the Life supported, are still discussed.

title: The Holy Rule of St. Benedict
subtitle: With his Life by St. Gregory the Great
author: St. Benedict of Nursia
lead: The rule for monks written by Benedict of Nursia at Monte Cassino in the sixth century, with the account of his life in the second book of the Dialogues of Gregory the Great.
description: Benedict was born at Nursia in Umbria about 480, left his studies at Rome for a hermit’s life at Subiaco, and later founded the monastery of Monte Cassino, between Rome and Naples, where he died about 547. He wrote the Rule there, probably in the 530s or 540s, drawing on earlier monastic writings, among them the anonymous Rule of the Master, Cassian and Basil. It has a Prologue and seventy-three chapters, on the abbot and the community, obedience, silence and humility, the order of the Divine Office by day and night, the correction of faults, manual work and reading, the reception of guests and of new brethren, and the choice of an abbot. Bound with it is the second book of Gregory the Great’s Dialogues, written about 593–594 and the only early account of Benedict’s life.

The Rule opens, “Listen, O my son, to the precepts of thy master, and incline the ear of thy heart,” and it orders a common life of prayer, work and reading under an abbot who holds the place of Christ in the monastery, with moderation in food, sleep and discipline. Its last chapter calls it a rule for beginners and sends the monk on to the Fathers, to Cassian and to the Rule of Basil. Through the reforms of Benedict of Aniane under the Carolingian emperors it became the rule of most monasteries in the West, and it remains the rule of the Benedictine and Cistercian orders. Anglican and Lutheran communities also live by it or draw on it, and Benedict is honoured as a saint in the Orthodox Church as well.

title: The Book of Pastoral Rule
author: St. Gregory the Great
lead: Gregory the Great’s book on the office of a bishop, who should take it, how he should live, how he should teach each kind of hearer and how he should keep watch on himself, written soon after he became pope in 590.
description: Gregory, born to a senatorial family at Rome about 540, had been prefect of the city, a monk and the papal envoy at Constantinople before he was chosen bishop of Rome in 590. He had tried to avoid the office, and he wrote the Pastoral Rule for a fellow bishop named John, who had reproached him for it, generally identified as the bishop of Ravenna. The book is in four parts. The first treats who should come to the government of souls and in what spirit, and the second the life of the pastor. The third, the longest, treats the manner of admonishing hearers of every condition, set out in contrasting pairs, men and women, the poor and the rich, the joyful and the sad, servants and masters, and many more. The fourth and shortest calls the pastor back to himself, lest his good work make him proud.

Gregory holds that “the government of souls is the art of arts,” a thought he takes from Gregory of Nazianzus, and that no one should teach it who has not first learned it. He asks that the pastor be pure in thought, foremost in action, discreet in silence and useful in speech, near to each in compassion and raised above all in contemplation, and that he suit his words to each hearer as a physician suits the remedy to the disease. The book was read from the first as a handbook for bishops. It was put into Greek by Anastasius of Antioch in Gregory’s lifetime, and King Alfred translated it into Old English about 890 and sent a copy to every bishop of his kingdom. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant pastors have used it since as a guide to preaching and the care of souls.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons and writers Gregory names, the offices of the Church in his day, and the Scripture he cites. Barmby’s notes are kept.

title: The Dialogues of St. Gregory the Great
author: St. Gregory the Great
lead: Gregory the Great’s four books of conversation with his deacon Peter on the holy men of Italy, their miracles and the life of the soul after death, written about 593–594.
description: Gregory was bishop of Rome from 590 to 604. In the prologue he tells how, worn down by the business of his office, he withdrew to a quiet place, where his deacon Peter found him and asked to hear of the holy men of Italy, whose wonders Peter thought less known than those of the East. The four books are his answer. The first tells of bishops, abbots and priests of the Italian Church, many known to Gregory through witnesses he names. The second is given wholly to Benedict of Nursia and is the only early account of his life. The third gathers further lives, among them martyrs of the Lombard invasions. The fourth turns to the soul, its life after death, the visions of the dying, and the help that prayer and the offering of the Mass can bring to the dead.

The Dialogues were among the most read books of the Middle Ages. Pope Zacharias put them into Greek in the eighth century, and from them Gregory is known in the Eastern Church as Gregory the Dialogist. Wærferth, bishop of Worcester, translated them into Old English at the request of King Alfred. In the West the fourth book, with its teaching on a cleansing fire after death for lesser faults and on the Eucharist offered for the departed, was cited for the doctrine of purgatory, which the Protestant Reformers rejected. In the East the Greek version was read in the monasteries, and the Orthodox Church honours Gregory as a saint. In the twentieth century a few scholars argued that the work was not Gregory’s, a view that most have not accepted.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons, places, monasteries and events of sixth-century Italy that Gregory names and on the Scripture he cites.

title: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
author: St. John of Damascus
lead: John of Damascus’s summary of the faith of the Greek Fathers and the councils, in a hundred chapters on God, creation, the Incarnation and the life of the Church, written in Palestine in the first half of the eighth century.
description: John was born at Damascus in the later seventh century to a Christian family that served the Muslim caliphs as financial officials, and he held office there himself before he became a monk, by tradition at the monastery of Mar Saba near Jerusalem. He died about 750. The Exact Exposition is the third part of his Fount of Knowledge, after the Philosophical Chapters, which set out the terms of logic, and the book On Heresies. The hundred chapters were divided into four books in the Latin translation made by Burgundio of Pisa in the twelfth century. The first treats God and the Trinity, the second creation, the angels, the world, man and providence, the third the Incarnation, the two natures and the two wills of Christ, and the fourth the risen Christ, faith and baptism, the Eucharist, the Mother of God, the saints, their relics and their images, the Scriptures and the last things.

John draws on Athanasius, the Cappadocians, Cyril of Alexandria, Maximus the Confessor and others, and he uses the terms of the councils from Nicaea to the Third Council of Constantinople. He teaches that the Spirit is from the Father and is called the Spirit of the Son, that the Virgin is rightly called Theotokos, that the bread and wine are changed into the body and blood of Christ, and that the honour given to an image passes to its prototype. In the Orthodox Church the work has long served as a summary of dogma. Peter Lombard used the Latin version in his Sentences and Thomas Aquinas cited it often, so that it shaped Western scholastic theology as well. Its chapters on the Spirit were cited on both sides of the dispute between East and West over the Filioque, and Protestant readers have studied it as a witness to Greek theology after the councils.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the Fathers, councils, heresies and philosophers John names and on the Scripture he cites. Salmond’s notes are kept.

title: Catena Aurea on St. Matthew
subtitle: Commentary on the Gospel collected out of the works of the Fathers
author: St. Thomas Aquinas
lead: The Gospel of Matthew expounded verse by verse in a chain of passages from the Greek and Latin Fathers, compiled by Thomas Aquinas for Pope Urban IV in the early 1260s.
description: Thomas Aquinas, the Dominican friar and master of theology, made the Catena Aurea, the “golden chain,” at the request of Pope Urban IV, to whom he presented the commentary on Matthew before the pope’s death in 1264. He went on to Mark, Luke and John, which he dedicated to Cardinal Annibaldo degli Annibaldi, and he finished the whole about 1268. The method is the same throughout. Under each verse or group of verses Thomas sets passages from the Fathers, each under its author’s name, abridged and joined so that they read as a continuous exposition, with the Gloss filling the gaps. The volume on Matthew opens with a prologue on Isaiah 40:9, “Go up to the top of the mountain, thou that preachest glad tidings in Sion,” and then follows the Gospel through its twenty-eight chapters.

Matthew was the Gospel the Fathers expounded most, and this is the longest of the four parts. Jerome’s commentary on Matthew and Chrysostom’s homilies on Matthew are cited most often, followed by Augustine, the unfinished commentary on Matthew long ascribed to Chrysostom, Remigius of Auxerre, Hilary of Poitiers, Origen and Rabanus Maurus, with Gregory the Great, Ambrose and Leo after them. The chain runs through the genealogy and the infancy, the Sermon on the Mount, the parables of the kingdom, the discourses on the end and the Passion, and where the Fathers differ Thomas sets them side by side. At the confession of Peter it gives their several readings of the rock on which Christ builds his Church: Peter, his confession of faith, and Christ himself. The commentary was used by preachers and teachers in the medieval West and printed many times from the fifteenth century, and since the Oxford translation it has been read in English by Catholic, Anglican and other readers.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the Fathers and later writers Thomas cites, the councils and heresies they name, and the Scripture they quote.

title: Catena Aurea on St. Mark
subtitle: Commentary on the Gospel collected out of the works of the Fathers
author: St. Thomas Aquinas
lead: The Gospel of Mark expounded verse by verse in a chain of passages from the Latin and Greek Fathers, compiled by Thomas Aquinas in the 1260s and dedicated to Cardinal Annibaldo degli Annibaldi.
description: After presenting his chain on Matthew to Pope Urban IV, Thomas Aquinas continued the work through the other three Gospels and dedicated them to Cardinal Annibaldo degli Annibaldi, a Dominican like himself. In the dedication he says that he had expositions of the Greek Doctors translated into Latin for the purpose, so that these later volumes draw on Greek writers little read in the Latin schools of his day. The volume on Mark opens with a prologue on Isaiah 49, in which Jerome and the Gloss explain the calling of the Gentiles, and Eusebius reports that Mark wrote down the preaching of Peter at Rome. It then follows the Gospel through its sixteen chapters, setting the Fathers’ words in order under each verse.

Few of the Fathers wrote on Mark, who was long read as an abridgement of Matthew, and the chain on Mark is the shortest of the four. Thomas leans most on Bede’s commentary on Mark, on Theophylact, the eleventh-century archbishop of Ohrid, whose Greek commentary on the Gospels he cites in Latin, and on a commentary on Mark then ascribed to Jerome and now thought to be the work of a later writer. Chrysostom, Augustine and the unfinished commentary on Matthew fill out the rest. The result is a reading of Mark’s narrative in its own order: the preaching of John the Baptist, the call of the disciples, the miracles and exorcisms in Galilee, the Transfiguration, the entry into Jerusalem, the Passion and the Resurrection. The Greek material in this volume, Theophylact above all, makes it one of the places where Latin readers met Byzantine exegesis, and it is read now by Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant students of the Fathers alike.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the Fathers and later writers Thomas cites, the councils and heresies they name, and the Scripture they quote.

title: Catena Aurea on St. Luke
subtitle: Commentary on the Gospel collected out of the works of the Fathers
author: St. Thomas Aquinas
lead: The Gospel of Luke expounded verse by verse in a chain of passages from the Latin and Greek Fathers, the third part of the Catena Aurea compiled by Thomas Aquinas in the 1260s.
description: Thomas Aquinas compiled the chain on Luke as the third part of the Catena Aurea, which he had begun at the request of Pope Urban IV and continued for Cardinal Annibaldo degli Annibaldi, finishing the whole about 1268. As in the other parts, each verse of the Gospel stands at the head of passages from the Fathers, set in an order that makes a running commentary. The prologue, on Isaiah 50, takes from Augustine and Ambrose the old figure of Luke as the calf, the priestly victim, because his Gospel begins with the priest Zacharias in the Temple, and it quotes Jerome on the polish of Luke’s Greek. The volume follows the twenty-four chapters of the Gospel and is the second longest of the four parts.

For Luke Thomas could draw on two full Latin commentaries, Ambrose’s Exposition of the Gospel of Luke and Bede’s commentary, and these two, with Theophylact, carry the larger part of the chain. Chrysostom, Augustine, Gregory the Great, Origen, Basil, Eusebius and Athanasius are cited after them, and many passages come from the Greek catenae under the heading of Greek expositors. The chain covers the passages only Luke gives: the annunciations to Zacharias and to Mary, the Magnificat and the Benedictus, the shepherds and the presentation in the Temple, the parables of the Good Samaritan, the prodigal son and the rich man and Lazarus, and the walk to Emmaus. Many of the Gospels read on the Sundays of the year are taken from Luke, and preachers in the Latin West used the chain as a guide to what the Fathers had said on them. Its chapters on the infancy have been read by Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers for the Fathers’ teaching on the Incarnation and on the Virgin.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the Fathers and later writers Thomas cites, the councils and heresies they name, and the Scripture they quote.

title: Catena Aurea on St. John
subtitle: Commentary on the Gospel collected out of the works of the Fathers
author: St. Thomas Aquinas
lead: The Gospel of John expounded verse by verse in a chain of passages from the Fathers, the last part of the Catena Aurea compiled by Thomas Aquinas in the 1260s.
description: The chain on John completes the commentary on the four Gospels that Thomas Aquinas began for Pope Urban IV and finished for Cardinal Annibaldo degli Annibaldi about 1268. This volume opens directly on the first verse of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the Fathers come at once to the eternal generation of the Son. Chrysostom observes that John, passing over the conception and the nativity, “speaks immediately of the Eternal Generation.” The volume then follows the twenty-one chapters of the Gospel, verse by verse. Thomas also lectured on John at Paris a few years later, and his own commentary on John is a separate work from this chain of the Fathers.

John’s Gospel had two great commentaries among the Fathers, Augustine’s tractates on John, preached at Hippo, and Chrysostom’s homilies on John, preached at Antioch, and between them they supply the larger part of this chain. Theophylact, Alcuin, Origen, Bede, Gregory the Great and Hilary are cited after them. Here the Fathers set out at length their teaching on the Trinity and on the person of Christ, much of it written against the Arians and others who denied that the Son is equal to the Father. The sixth chapter gathers their readings of the discourse on the Bread of Life, which Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers have long weighed in their differing teaching on the Eucharist, and the chapters on the Last Supper gather their readings of Christ’s farewell discourses and his prayer for his disciples.

No. 22 of Lérins Fathers prints the Catena on John in the Oxford translation edited by John Henry Newman, published by John Henry Parker between 1841 and 1845, the volume on John being the last of the four. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the Fathers and later writers Thomas cites, the councils and heresies they name, and the Scripture they quote.

title: The Confessions of St. Augustine
author: St. Augustine
lead: Augustine’s account of his life to the year of his conversion, told as a prayer addressed to God, written as bishop of Hippo in North Africa about 397–400.
description: Augustine became bishop of Hippo in 396 and wrote the Confessions within a few years of it, some ten years after his conversion at Milan in 386. The book is spoken throughout to God, and its readers overhear it. Its thirteen books fall into two parts. Books 1 to 9 follow his life from infancy at Thagaste through his schooling at Carthage, his nine years among the Manichees, his teaching of rhetoric at Rome and Milan, the preaching of Ambrose, the garden at Milan where he heard a child’s voice chanting “Take up and read,” his baptism at Easter 387, and the death of his mother Monica at Ostia. Book 10 turns to his present state and to memory. Books 11 to 13 read the opening of Genesis, with long inquiries into time and creation.

The Confessions treats a single life as evidence of the grace of God, who in Augustine’s telling was at work in him long before he turned. It names his sins, his errors and his friendships, and it asks what a man is and how he can find God within himself. Its first chapter gives the sentence most often taken from it: “Thou hast formed us for Thyself, and our hearts are restless till they find rest in Thee.” The book has been read without a break since Augustine’s lifetime. Medieval monks, Petrarch and the Reformers all drew on it. It remains a standard text for Catholic and Protestant readers alike, while Orthodox readers, who honour Augustine as a saint, have received his wider theology with more reserve.

Pilkington, first published at Edinburgh in 1876 and reissued in 1886 in the first series of A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, edited by Philip Schaff, from the text kept in the site’s library. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons and places of Augustine’s life, the Manichees and Platonists he read, the Scripture he quotes, and the terms of his teaching on grace, memory and time.

title: The Cloud of Unknowing
lead: An anonymous English guide to contemplative prayer, written in the second half of the fourteenth century by a priest whose name is lost.
description: The Cloud of Unknowing was written in the English of the East Midlands in the later fourteenth century. Its author does not give his name, and none of the many guesses made since has been proved. He addresses the book to a single disciple whom he believes called to the contemplative life, and in a prologue he asks that it be read only by those so called and by no one else. The same author wrote other short works, among them The Book of Privy Counselling, which answers questions raised by the Cloud, and an English version of the Mystical Theology of Dionysius, the writer on whose teaching the Cloud chiefly draws. The work survives in a number of manuscripts and is laid out in seventy-five short chapters.

The author teaches that God cannot be reached by thinking, however holy the thought, but can be reached by love. Between the soul and God lies a cloud of unknowing, and the soul is to beat upon it with a “naked intent” toward God. Below the soul it is to put everything else, creatures, deeds and even good thoughts, under a cloud of forgetting. A short word such as “God” or “love” may be held in the mind to gather the intent. In the seventeenth century the English Benedictine Augustine Baker commented on the book, and its manuscripts were kept among English Catholic religious in exile. In the twentieth century Anglican and Catholic writers on prayer took it up again, and the Trappist teachers of centering prayer drew directly on it. It is now read by Christians of many churches.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons and Scripture the author names, the writings of Dionysius behind him, and the terms of the medieval English contemplative tradition.

title: Revelations of Divine Love
author: Julian of Norwich
lead: The showings of Julian of Norwich, sixteen visions received in May 1373 and the long reflection on them that she wrote in the following decades in her anchorhold at Norwich.
description: In May 1373, when she was thirty and a half years old, Julian fell so ill that she and those around her expected her to die. A priest held a crucifix before her eyes, and over the next hours she received a series of sixteen showings, most of them concerning the Passion of Christ and the love of God. She recovered, and wrote a short account of what she had seen soon afterwards, and some twenty years later a far longer text in eighty-six chapters, the fruit of long thought about what the showings meant. For much of her life she lived as an anchoress in a cell joined to the church of St. Julian at Conisford in Norwich, and she is probably known by the church’s name. Her book is the earliest surviving book in English known to have been written by a woman. The long text was first printed in 1670 by the English Benedictine Serenus Cressy.

Julian speaks of the goodness of God, who made all things, loves all things and keeps them in being, and she describes being shown the whole of creation as a thing the size of a hazelnut in the palm of her hand. She writes of sin and its pain, of the mercy that meets it, and of the motherhood of Christ, and she reports the promise given her that all shall be well. Little read for centuries, her book has been widely read since the early twentieth century. She is commemorated on 8 May in the calendars of the Church of England and other Anglican churches and of several Lutheran churches. In the Catholic Church she has never been formally canonised, but she is honoured, and Pope Benedict XVI gave a general audience on her teaching in 2010.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons, places and Scripture Julian names, the life of an anchoress, and the terms of her theology of sin, mercy and the love of God.

title: The Imitation of Christ
author: Thomas à Kempis
lead: Four books of counsel on the inward life and the sacrament of the altar, written in Latin in the early fifteenth century by Thomas à Kempis, a canon regular at Mount St. Agnes near Zwolle.
description: Thomas Hemerken was born at Kempen in the Rhineland about 1380 and schooled at Deventer among the Brethren of the Common Life, the movement of the Low Countries known as the devotio moderna. He entered the house of Augustinian canons at Mount St. Agnes near Zwolle, where he spent most of his long life as a copyist, preacher and director of novices, and where he died in 1471. The four books of the Imitation circulated first without an author’s name, as separate treatises, and were gathered together in the early fifteenth century. A manuscript in Thomas’s hand, dated 1441, is kept in the Royal Library at Brussels. The book was later claimed for other writers, among them Jean Gerson, and its authorship was argued over for centuries. Most scholars now credit it to Thomas.

The first book gives counsels useful for the spiritual life, the second concerns the inward life, the third is a long dialogue between Christ and the disciple on inward consolation, and the fourth prepares the reader to receive the Eucharist. Its teaching is that the Christian should follow Christ in humility, contempt of worldly vanity, patience under trial and love of the cross, and seek peace in God rather than in learning or the opinion of others. It has been printed in more editions than almost any other Christian book apart from the Bible. Ignatius of Loyola made it his daily reading, and Catholic religious have used it for centuries. John Wesley published his own translation in 1735 as The Christian’s Pattern, and it has been read by Anglicans, Lutherans and other Protestants as well as Catholics, often with the fourth book omitted or set apart.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the Scripture Thomas quotes and echoes, the life of the devotio moderna and its houses, and the terms of its teaching on the inward life and the sacrament.

title: The Interior Castle
author: St. Teresa of Ávila
lead: Teresa of Ávila’s account of the soul as a castle of seven mansions, through which it passes inward toward union with God, written for her Discalced Carmelite nuns in 1577.
description: Teresa wrote the Interior Castle in 1577, at the command of her superior Jerónimo Gracián, at a time when the reform of the Carmelite order she had begun was under attack and the book of her Life was in the hands of the Inquisition. She began it at Toledo in June and finished it at Ávila in November, with a long break between. It was written for the nuns of her reformed convents, and she says in it that she writes for them. The book takes the form of seven mansions, or dwelling places, each divided into chapters, and the autograph is kept by the Discalced Carmelite nuns of Seville. It was first printed at Salamanca in 1588, six years after her death, in the edition of her works prepared by the Augustinian friar Luis de León.

Teresa compares the soul to a castle made of a single diamond or of very clear crystal, with many rooms, and God dwelling at its centre. Prayer is the door by which the soul enters. The first three mansions describe the efforts of a soul that is learning to pray and to keep from sin. The fourth begins the prayer that God gives rather than the soul achieves, and the last three describe the betrothal and spiritual marriage of the soul with God, in which, she writes, the soul does not cease from work and service of others. Teresa was canonised in 1622, and in 1970 she became the first woman named a Doctor of the Church. The book is a standard text on prayer in the Catholic Church and has been widely read by Anglicans, Protestants and other Christians.

The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons and places of Teresa’s reform, the Scripture she uses, and the terms of her teaching on prayer, the mansions and union with God.

title: The Dark Night of the Soul
author: St. John of the Cross
lead: John of the Cross’s poem of eight stanzas on the soul’s going out by night to meet God, with his prose commentary on its purification, written in Spain in the 1580s.
description: Juan de Yepes was born at Fontiveros in Castile in 1542 and joined the Carmelites, and in 1568 he became one of the first friars of the reform begun by Teresa of Ávila. In December 1577 friars opposed to the reform carried him off to their house at Toledo and held him in a cell for more than eight months, until he escaped in August 1578. The poem that opens “En una noche oscura,” “On a dark night,” is commonly dated to the time of that imprisonment or the years just after it. In the 1580s, in Andalusia, he wrote a commentary on it for the friars and nuns he directed. The commentary is in two books, on the night of sense and the night of spirit, and it breaks off at the beginning of the third stanza. John died at Úbeda in 1591, and his prose works were first printed at Alcalá in 1618.

John teaches that God, to bring a soul to union with Himself, leads it through darkness. In the night of sense He takes away the comfort it found in prayer and devotion, so that it may love Him and not His gifts. In the night of spirit He purifies its very understanding, memory and will, and the soul suffers this as a dark and painful light. The poem presents the same passage as a lover going out unseen by night to meet the one she loves. John was canonised in 1726 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1926. The Catholic Church holds his writings as a standard of mystical theology, they have been read widely by Anglicans and Protestants, and the phrase “the dark night of the soul” has passed into common speech.

No. 6 of Lérins Devotions will print the Dark Night in the translation of David Lewis, first published in London in 1864 in The Complete Works of St. John of the Cross, with a preface by Cardinal Wiseman. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons and places of the Carmelite reform, the Scripture John quotes, and the terms of his teaching on the nights of sense and spirit.

title: Introduction to the Devout Life
author: St. Francis de Sales
lead: Francis de Sales’s guide to a devout life lived in the world, addressed to “Philothea,” first published at Lyon in 1609 by the bishop of Geneva.
description: Francis de Sales was born in Savoy in 1567, studied at Paris and Padua, and was ordained priest in 1593. He spent several years preaching in the Chablais, south of Lake Geneva, and in 1602 he became bishop of Geneva, living at Annecy because Geneva itself was Calvinist. The Introduction grew out of the notes of direction he wrote for Louise de Charmoisy, a married woman at the court of Savoy, which she showed to others. At their urging he gathered and enlarged them, and the book was published at Lyon in 1609. He revised it several times, and the final text appeared in 1619. He addresses his reader as Philothea, a name meaning one who loves God, and arranges the book in five parts, which lead from the first desire of devotion through prayer and the sacraments, the virtues, and the resisting of temptation, to a yearly renewal of the soul’s resolutions.

Francis holds that devotion is not for monks and nuns only. It is the love of God made prompt and active, and it belongs to every state of life, the soldier, the tradesman, the prince and the married woman, each in the manner fitting that state. He gives plain counsel on meditation, confession and Communion, on friendship, dress, conversation and amusements, and on bearing with one’s own faults. The book was translated into many languages within his lifetime. Francis was canonised in 1665 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1877. It has been used by Catholics as a manual of the spiritual life since it appeared, and English Protestants and Anglicans read adapted versions of it from the seventeenth century onward.
