The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons and places Francis names, the Scripture and the Fathers he cites, and the terms of his teaching on devotion, prayer and the sacraments.

title: The Practice of the Presence of God
subtitle: With Abandonment to Divine Providence
author: Brother Lawrence and Jean-Pierre de Caussade
lead: Two French writings on prayer in the round of daily work: the conversations, letters and maxims of Brother Lawrence, a Carmelite lay brother in Paris who died in 1691, and Abandonment to Divine Providence, from the teaching of the Jesuit Jean-Pierre de Caussade.
description: Nicolas Herman was born in Lorraine about 1614, served as a soldier in the Thirty Years’ War, and about 1640 entered the house of the Discalced Carmelites in Paris as a lay brother, taking the name Lawrence of the Resurrection. He worked for years in its kitchen and later as its sandal-maker, and died there in 1691. He wrote no book. After his death Joseph de Beaufort, vicar general to the bishop of Châlons, gathered his Spiritual Maxims and his letters, and published accounts of four conversations he had held with him. Jean-Pierre de Caussade, born in 1675, was a Jesuit who in the 1730s served as spiritual director to the Visitation nuns at Nancy. He died at Toulouse in 1751. The nuns kept copies of his letters and of a treatise on abandonment, and the Jesuit Henri Ramière published the treatise under his name in 1861. Some modern scholars have questioned how much of it is his.

Brother Lawrence describes a life of continual conversation with God, kept up among the pots and pans as much as in the chapel. He tells how he learned, after years of difficulty, to turn his mind back to God whenever it wandered and to do each small thing for love of Him. Caussade teaches that God is at work in each present moment and in every event, and that holiness lies in accepting the duty and the trial each moment brings as the will of God. Both are read far beyond the Catholic Church, and Brother Lawrence above all has been printed in English for Protestant readers since the eighteenth century.

No. 8 of Lérins Devotions will bind the two works in one volume. It prints Brother Lawrence’s Conversations and Letters in an English translation of the nineteenth century, with his Spiritual Maxims, and then Abandonment to Divine Providence in the translation of Ella McMahon, published in New York in 1887 from the eighth French edition. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons and religious houses named, the Scripture both writers use, and the terms of their teaching on prayer, providence and the present moment.

title: A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life
author: William Law
lead: William Law’s argument that the whole of a Christian’s life, and not only the hours of worship, is to be given to God, published in London in 1729.
description: William Law was born at King’s Cliffe in Northamptonshire in 1686 and became a fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge. On the accession of George I in 1714 he refused the oath of allegiance, holding himself bound by his earlier oaths to the Stuarts, and so became a nonjuror and lost his fellowship and any prospect of office in the Church of England. He was for some years tutor in the household of Edward Gibbon, father of the historian, at Putney, and in his later years he returned to King’s Cliffe, where he died in 1761. A Serious Call appeared in 1729. Its twenty-four chapters mix argument with short portraits of men and women under invented names, such as Flavia, whose religion is a matter of form, and her sister Miranda, who gives her life to God.

Law holds that devotion is not a set of religious acts added to an ordinary life but the ordering of the whole of it, money, time, work, dress and pleasures, to the glory of God. He presses this on every class of reader, the tradesman and the gentleman, the wealthy woman and the scholar, and he closes with a scheme of prayer through the day, assigning each hour its own subject, from thanksgiving at rising to humility, intercession and resignation to the will of God. The book had a large effect in its century. John and Charles Wesley read it at Oxford, and John Wesley visited Law at Putney. Samuel Johnson told Boswell that reading it at Oxford was the first occasion of his thinking in earnest of religion. It has since been read chiefly by Anglicans, Methodists and other Protestants.

No. 9 of Lérins Devotions will print A Serious Call in the text Law published in 1729. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons and places of Law’s England, the Scripture he cites, and the terms of his teaching on devotion, prayer and the Christian’s use of the world.

title: The Story of a Soul
subtitle: The autobiography of St. Thérèse of Lisieux
author: St. Thérèse of Lisieux
lead: The autobiography of Thérèse of Lisieux, a Carmelite nun who died at twenty-four in 1897, written in three parts at her superiors’ request and published a year after her death.
description: Thérèse Martin was born at Alençon in 1873, the youngest of nine children of Louis and Zélie Martin, and entered the Carmel of Lisieux in April 1888, at fifteen, where two of her sisters were already nuns. In 1895 her sister Pauline, then prioress as Mother Agnes of Jesus, asked her to write down her memories of childhood. In September 1896 she wrote a second part for her eldest sister Marie, and in June 1897, by then gravely ill with tuberculosis, a third for the prioress, Mother Marie de Gonzague. She died on 30 September 1897. Mother Agnes edited the three manuscripts into a single book, Histoire d’une âme, and it was printed in 1898 for the convents of the order. It was soon read far beyond them, and within a few years it had been translated into many languages.

Thérèse describes what she calls her little way: a life of trust and self-surrender to God like that of a small child to its father, in which small acts done with love count for much and the soul offers its weakness rather than great deeds. She writes of her childhood, her vocation, her love for the missions and the priesthood, and, in her last eighteen months, of a darkness of faith in which she kept believing. She was canonised in 1925 and in 1927 named a patron of the missions. In 1997 she was declared a Doctor of the Church. The book has been one of the most widely read Catholic works of the twentieth century, and it has also found readers among Anglican and Protestant Christians.

No. 10 of Lérins Devotions will print the autobiography in the translation of Thomas N. Taylor, priest of the Archdiocese of Glasgow and a witness in the process for her beatification, published in London in 1912. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons and places of Thérèse’s life, the Carmelite customs she describes, the Scripture she quotes, and the terms of her teaching.

title: The Pursuit of God
author: A. W. Tozer
lead: A. W. Tozer’s short book on seeking a personal knowledge of God beyond correct belief, written by a Chicago pastor of the Christian and Missionary Alliance and published in 1948.
description: Aiden Wilson Tozer was born in rural Pennsylvania in 1897 and became a Christian as a young man at Akron, Ohio. Without college or seminary training he was ordained in the Christian and Missionary Alliance, and from 1928 to 1959 he was pastor of the Southside Alliance Church in Chicago. He later moved to Toronto, where he died in 1963. According to his biographers, The Pursuit of God was written overnight on a train from Chicago to McAllen, Texas, where he was going to preach, and the draft was finished when the train arrived. It was published in 1948 by Christian Publications of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, the Alliance’s press. It has ten chapters, from “Following Hard after God” to “The Sacrament of Living.”

Tozer argues that many Christians who hold sound doctrine know God only at second hand, and that God may and should be known personally and continually. He writes of giving up possessions of the heart, of the veil of self that stands between the soul and God, of the presence of God everywhere, of His speaking voice, of faith as the gaze of the soul upon God, and of living each ordinary act as an offering to God. He draws freely on writers outside his own tradition, among them Nicholas of Cusa and the hymn writer Frederick Faber. The book has been read chiefly among evangelical Protestants, where it has been continuously in print since it appeared, and it has also found readers in other churches.

No. 11 of Lérins Devotions will print The Pursuit of God in the text of the first edition of 1948, with Tozer’s preface, dated at Chicago on 16 June 1948, and the introduction by Samuel M. Zwemer. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons Tozer cites, the Scripture he uses, and the terms of his teaching on the knowledge and presence of God.

title: Machines of Borrowed Grace
subtitle: Where a Language Model Gets Its Meaning, and Where Its Makers Get Theirs
author: Anonymous
lead: Whether a machine can think is a question about what it is for anything to mean something.
Language models now do work that used to take a mind. What are they, where do their words get their meaning, and what are the companies building them standing on?
description: This book asks what large language models actually are, where the meaning in their sentences comes from, and what the companies building them are relying on. It treats the machines as signs from end to end, numbers and tokens that mean something only because people trained them and people read them. It walks through ordinary examples like a word, a sum, a thermostat, and a sieve to show why the models can outperform most of us at coding, writing, and problem-solving without possessing a mind of their own. The first half stays close to the machine: how a sign comes to mean anything, whether a machine can think or feel, whether it can improve itself into understanding, and what would count as proof that it had. The second half turns to the people who make and sell the models, looking at the visions they offer of a future shaped by AI and the unstated assumptions those visions rest on.

The writing is plain and conversational, starting from everyday observations and building outward in the manner of Herbert McCabe explaining Aquinas. It draws mainly on Aristotle and Aquinas, with substantial help from Wittgenstein and more recent philosophers such as James Ross, while keeping technical claims about language models and their training tied to public sources. The author is explicit about working from a classical Christian frame, and the book moves from the philosophy of mind into questions of moral alignment, human dignity, and what a healed or flourishing human life would look like once AI is widespread.

Readers curious about AI beyond benchmark scores, especially those who wonder whether the technology requires any revision of older ideas about thought, meaning, or human nature, will find a sustained and accessible treatment here. It is less a technical survey of current models than a philosophical map of the territory the models occupy, written for anyone who wants to think through the claims that the machine understands, that alignment is the hard part, or that AI will deliver the good life, without needing prior training in either philosophy or machine learning.

title: Mere Catholicity
subtitle: The Common Faith of East and West
author: Anonymous
lead: For the layman, it is all about 1054. The great wound in Christendom is not the changes of the last century. It is the Great Schism of 1054, when East and West tore apart, and so much of the later tearing follows from it.
description: For the layman, it is all about 1054. The great wound in Christendom is not the changes of the last century. It is the Great Schism of 1054, when East and West tore apart, and so much of the later tearing follows from it. The faith of the first thousand years is the ground the ancient churches still share. What each side defined after the tear it defined alone, and what a part defines alone cannot bind the whole until the whole comes to confess it. This book is a call to walk back, past every later rupture, to that first faith, and it is addressed to every house that still keeps a part of it, Roman, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Presbyterian.

For the theologian, the thesis is this. A council binds when the whole Body comes to confess the faith it defined, and binding by act alone never existed in the conciliar age, for the Body has been torn since 251 and reception across the open tears is attested wherever it has been checked. The church that refused Ephesus confesses, in Babai, the one Christ Ephesus defined. The churches that refused Chalcedon confess, in Severus, the faith it guarded. Measured by that record, the definitions added since the great schisms, Vatican I and the Marian dogmas on one side, the Palamite councils on the other, stand not yet received, never condemned, and the book denies both communions the same thing, the identification of the whole with a part. It keeps Newman's method while declining his authority, claims Ratzinger's Graz formula as lineage, quotes the ex sese clause rather than paraphrasing it and stands under its anathema, grades every disputed act of both millennia in an appendix, and lets its own rules cut against its own comfort, usury the hardest case, the veil left binding unless a retraction is shown. It closes with a proposal in Zoghby's genre made mutual, synodal professions by which each communion holds its post-schism definitions as patrimony rather than exacting them as conditions of communion.

And if this is true, then Tolkien and Lewis, the Roman Catholic and the Anglican who between them taught the last century's laymen to love the permanent things, are not divided now as they were at every altar on earth, and may well be smoking their pipes side by side in heaven, having a laugh with Luther, who swore he would sooner drink the blood of Christ with the papists than mere wine with the fanatics. And Dostoevsky is there too, the Orthodox among them, who always suspected heaven would be more crowded than the experts allowed. The hope of this confession is not more complicated than that.

title: The Surprising Work of God
subtitle: A Faithful Narrative, The Distinguishing Marks, and Some Thoughts Concerning the Present Revival
author: Jonathan Edwards
lead: Jonathan Edwards’s own account of the revival in New England, in three works written at Northampton, Massachusetts, between 1737 and 1743.
description: Jonathan Edwards was born in 1703 at East Windsor, Connecticut, and studied at Yale. In 1727 he joined his grandfather Solomon Stoddard as minister of Northampton, Massachusetts, and succeeded him there in 1729. In 1734 and 1735 a revival passed through the town and the Connecticut valley, and at the request of ministers in Boston and London Edwards described it in A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God, printed in London in 1737. When the larger awakening came in 1740 and 1741, after George Whitefield’s preaching tour, it divided the churches of New England, and Edwards wrote twice more in its defence and correction.

The volume binds the three works whole, in the order written. A Faithful Narrative (1737) tells the course of the Northampton revival and the conversions in it, among them those of Abigail Hutchinson and the child Phebe Bartlet. The Distinguishing Marks of a Work of the Spirit of God (1741), enlarged from a sermon preached at Yale’s commencement, sets out from the First Epistle of John the signs by which a true work of God may be known, and the signs that prove nothing either way. Some Thoughts Concerning the Present Revival of Religion in New England (1743) answers its critics, chiefly Charles Chauncy of Boston, and warns its friends against the excesses that were discrediting it.

No. 1 of Lérins America, in the first part of the collection, the Great Awakening, 1737–1758, binds the three works in the texts of their first editions, with their original prefaces, among them the preface to the Narrative signed in London by Isaac Watts and John Guyse. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the two revivals and the pamphlet war the second raised, and explanatory notes on the persons and towns Edwards names, the critics he answers, and the Scripture he expounds. Religious Affections, No. 3, carries the same inquiry to its full length.

title: Journals and Sermons
subtitle: The American Journals, with Select Sermons
author: George Whitefield
lead: George Whitefield’s journals of his first American journeys, from 1738 to 1741, with a selection of the sermons he preached on them.
description: George Whitefield was born at Gloucester in 1714 and went up to Pembroke College, Oxford, where he joined the society of John and Charles Wesley that their critics called the Holy Club. Ordained in the Church of England in 1736, he became within two years the most sought-after preacher in England, and when the churches closed their pulpits to him he preached in the open air. He crossed the Atlantic thirteen times. His second American journey, from 1739 to 1741, took him from Georgia to New England, and the crowds that heard him there are commonly counted the beginning of the Great Awakening. He died at Newburyport, Massachusetts, in 1770.

Whitefield kept a journal of his travels and published it in parts as he went. The parts printed here cover his first voyage to Georgia in 1738 and the long tour of 1739 to 1741: his preaching in Philadelphia, New York and Charleston, the founding of the orphan house he called Bethesda near Savannah, his meetings with Jonathan Edwards at Northampton and with Benjamin Franklin at Philadelphia, and the opposition of the clergy who refused him their churches. With them are sermons he printed in those years, among them those he preached most often.

No. 2 of Lérins America, in the first part of the collection, the Great Awakening, 1737–1758, prints the American parts of the Journals whole, at Whitefield’s own divisions and in the texts of their first printings, with a selection of the sermons he published in the same years. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Whitefield’s life, his preaching and the controversy over the Journals in England and America, and explanatory notes on the persons, colonies and churches he names, the clergy who opposed him, and the Scripture he preaches. Edwards’s account of the same revival is No. 1.

title: Religious Affections
subtitle: A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections, in Three Parts
author: Jonathan Edwards
lead: Jonathan Edwards’s treatise of 1746 on how true religion may be told from false, written after the Great Awakening had divided New England.
description: By 1742 the Great Awakening had left New England divided between those who saw in it a work of God and those who saw only enthusiasm. Edwards, who had defended the revival, preached a series of sermons at Northampton in 1742 and 1743 on the First Epistle of Peter, “whom having not seen, ye love”, asking what marks a true work of grace in the soul. He revised them into A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections, published at Boston in 1746. Four years later his congregation dismissed him, in a dispute over the terms of admission to communion.

The treatise is in three parts. The first argues that true religion lies very much in the affections, the strong inclinations of the will toward or away from what the mind perceives. The second lists signs that prove nothing either way: intense feeling, bodily effects, fluent talk of religion, texts coming suddenly to mind, confidence of one’s own good estate. The third, the longest, gives twelve signs of gracious affections, from their divine origin to the last and chief of them, a life of Christian practice. Edwards quotes the Puritans throughout, above all Thomas Shepard, John Flavel and John Owen.

No. 3 of Lérins America, in the first part of the collection, the Great Awakening, 1737–1758, prints the Treatise whole, in the text of the first edition of Boston, 1746, with Edwards’s preface and his own notes as he left them. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the treatise’s making in the aftermath of the revival, and explanatory notes on the Puritan authors Edwards quotes, the parties of the Awakening, and the terms of his account of the understanding, the will and the affections. His earlier writings on the revival are No. 1, and his Life of David Brainerd, No. 4, was meant as its illustration in a single life.

title: The Life of David Brainerd
subtitle: Chiefly Extracted from His Diary
author: David Brainerd and Jonathan Edwards
lead: The diary of a young missionary to the Native Americans of New York, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, published by Jonathan Edwards in 1749 with his own reflections.
description: David Brainerd was born at Haddam, Connecticut, in 1718. He was converted in 1739 and entered Yale, but was expelled in 1742 for a remark about a tutor during the revival. Commissioned by the Society in Scotland for Propagating Christian Knowledge, he worked among the Mahicans at Kaunaumeek in New York, then among the Delawares at the Forks of the Delaware in Pennsylvania and at Crossweeksung in New Jersey, where in 1745 and 1746 a large part of the community became Christian. Ill with tuberculosis, he came to Edwards’s house at Northampton in 1747 and died there in October, at twenty-nine.

Brainerd left his diaries to Edwards, who edited them and published An Account of the Life of the Late Reverend Mr. David Brainerd at Boston in 1749. The book follows Brainerd in his own words from his conversion to his death: his journeys on horseback through the forests, his preaching through interpreters, his loneliness, his fasts and his long seasons of prayer and of dejection. Edwards adds connecting narrative and a closing set of reflections on what the life shows of true religion. The book was read by generations of missionaries after him, William Carey and Henry Martyn among them.

No. 4 of Lérins America, in the first part of the collection, the Great Awakening, 1737–1758, prints Edwards’s edition of 1749 whole, with his preface and his closing reflections, not the enlarged edition of 1822 that later reprints follow. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Brainerd’s life and mission and on Edwards’s purpose in publishing the diary, and explanatory notes on the persons, places and peoples Brainerd names, the missionary society that sent him, the dispute that cost him his degree, and the Scripture of the diary.

title: Freedom of the Will
subtitle: A Careful and Strict Enquiry into the Modern Prevailing Notions of That Freedom of Will
author: Jonathan Edwards
lead: Jonathan Edwards’s inquiry of 1754 into the freedom of the will, written at the mission town of Stockbridge against the Arminian writers of his day.
description: Dismissed from Northampton in 1750, Edwards went in 1751 to Stockbridge, then a frontier mission town in western Massachusetts, as pastor to its English settlers and its Mahican and Mohawk people. There he wrote the works his reputation as a philosopher chiefly rests on. The first was A Careful and Strict Enquiry into the Modern Prevailing Notions of that Freedom of Will which is Supposed to be Essential to Moral Agency, published at Boston in 1754. Its opponents are named on its pages: Thomas Chubb, Daniel Whitby and Isaac Watts.

Edwards defines the will as that by which the mind chooses, and argues that it is always determined by what seems to the mind the greatest apparent good. Against the view that freedom requires the will to determine itself, he argues that such self-determination is incoherent, and that liberty is the power to do as one wills. He then argues that necessity of this kind is consistent with moral responsibility, with praise and blame, with God’s commands and with the use of means, and answers the objections that it makes God the author of sin. The book is in four parts and closes with a summary of its conclusions.

No. 5 of Lérins America, in the first part of the collection, the Great Awakening, 1737–1758, prints the Enquiry whole, in the text of the first edition of Boston, 1754, with Edwards’s preface and the four parts and conclusion as he arranged them. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the years at Stockbridge and the debate Edwards entered, and explanatory notes on Chubb, Whitby and Watts as he quotes them, on Locke and the other philosophers he assumes, and on the terms of his argument, with the Scripture he cites. Original Sin, No. 6, is its companion.

title: Original Sin
subtitle: The Great Christian Doctrine of Original Sin Defended
author: Jonathan Edwards
lead: Jonathan Edwards’s defence of the doctrine of original sin against John Taylor of Norwich, published at Boston in 1758, the year of his death.
description: In 1740 John Taylor, a Presbyterian minister at Norwich in England, published The Scripture-Doctrine of Original Sin, arguing that the doctrine was neither scriptural nor reasonable. The book was widely read in New England. Edwards answered it at Stockbridge in The Great Christian Doctrine of Original Sin Defended. In January 1758 he became president of the College of New Jersey at Princeton, and in March he died there after inoculation against smallpox, while the book was in the press.

The treatise is in four parts. The first argues from the evidence of history and experience that mankind is universally inclined to sin. The second and third examine the testimony of Scripture, chiefly the third chapter of Genesis and the fifth chapter of Romans. The fourth answers objections, and in it Edwards gives his account of how all mankind is one with Adam, by a constitution of God that makes the race one moral whole, as he holds that God’s continual creation makes each person one through time. The work quotes Taylor at length and answers him point by point.

No. 6 of Lérins America, in the first part of the collection, the Great Awakening, 1737–1758, prints the treatise whole, in the text of the first edition of Boston, 1758, with Edwards’s preface. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Taylor’s book and its reception in New England and on the last months of Edwards’s life, and explanatory notes on the arguments Edwards quotes, the divines on either side, and the Scripture the debate turns on. Freedom of the Will, No. 5, is its companion.

title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
subtitle: with The Way to Wealth and Other Essays
author: Benjamin Franklin
lead: Benjamin Franklin’s account of his own life, from his boyhood in Boston to 1757, with The Way to Wealth and a selection of his essays.
description: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706, the fifteenth child of a candle maker, and ran away to Philadelphia at seventeen. He became its leading printer, the publisher of Poor Richard’s Almanack, a scientist known across Europe for his experiments with electricity, and a founder of its library, its fire company and its academy. He signed the Declaration of Independence, negotiated the alliance with France and the peace with Britain, and sat in the Constitutional Convention. He began his memoirs in 1771 in England, addressed to his son, and added to them in France in 1784 and at Philadelphia in 1788 and 1789. He died in 1790.

The Autobiography tells his apprenticeship to his brother in Boston, his arrival in Philadelphia with a few coins, his years in London as a journeyman printer, his rise in business, his plan for arriving at moral perfection by thirteen virtues, and his public projects, and breaks off in 1757. It was first printed entire in English from his manuscript by John Bigelow in 1868. With it is The Way to Wealth (1758), the speech of Father Abraham made of Poor Richard’s proverbs, and a selection of his essays, among them his speech at the close of the Convention in 1787.

No. 7 of Lérins America, the first of the collection’s second part, the Founding and the Republic, 1771–1799, numbered by the year Franklin began it, prints the Autobiography whole in the text Bigelow took from the manuscript in 1868, with The Way to Wealth and a selection of the essays. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the writing of the memoirs and the history of their text, and explanatory notes on the persons, places and institutions Franklin names, the colonial politics he describes, and his own later life beyond the point where he stopped.

title: Common Sense · The American Crisis
author: Thomas Paine
lead: Thomas Paine’s pamphlet of January 1776 for American independence, and the sixteen papers he wrote through the war that followed.
description: Thomas Paine was born at Thetford in Norfolk in 1737 and worked as a corset maker and an excise officer before he came to Philadelphia in 1774 with a letter of introduction from Benjamin Franklin. In January 1776, with the colonies at war with Britain but still professing loyalty to the King, he published Common Sense, which argued for independence and a republic. It sold in tens of thousands within months and was read aloud in taverns and camps. He served in the army and in Congress, and later took part in the French Revolution. He died in New York in 1809.

Common Sense attacks monarchy and hereditary succession, argues that reconciliation with Britain is impossible and against America’s interest, and sets out a plan of continental government. The volume prints the enlarged edition of February 1776, with its Appendix and its Address to the Quakers. The American Crisis is the series of sixteen papers Paine wrote from December 1776 to 1783, the first of them, which opens “These are the times that try men’s souls”, read to Washington’s army before it crossed the Delaware.

No. 8 of Lérins America, in the second part of the collection, the Founding and the Republic, 1771–1799, prints both works whole: Common Sense in the enlarged edition of February 1776, and The American Crisis in all sixteen of its numbers, as Paine dated them. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Paine’s life and the reception of his pamphlets, and explanatory notes on the persons, battles and events he names, the British ministers and loyalist writers he answers, and the Scripture he turns against monarchy. The Declaration of Independence, which followed Common Sense by six months, is in No. 9.

title: The Founding Documents
subtitle: The Declaration of Independence, the Articles of Confederation, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights
author: Founding Fathers
lead: The state papers of the American founding, from the Mayflower Compact to the Twelfth Amendment, each printed whole from its official text.
description: The United States was made by a series of written instruments: covenants among settlers, declarations of rights, a declaration of independence, a league of states, a treaty of peace, statutes, and at last a constitution amended by a bill of rights. They were drafted in assemblies and committees, revised in debate and adopted by vote, and many hands are in each. This volume gathers them in the order they were made, so a reader may follow the founding in the documents themselves.

It holds the Mayflower Compact (1620), the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), the Declaration of Independence (1776), the Articles of Confederation (1777), the Treaty of Paris (1783), the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom (1786), the Northwest Ordinance (1787), the Constitution (1787) with the names of its signers, the Bill of Rights (1791), and the Eleventh and Twelfth Amendments. Each is printed whole, from its official text.

No. 9 of Lérins America, in the second part of the collection, the Founding and the Republic, 1771–1799, prints the documents whole, in the order they were made, each from its official text, the Constitution with the names of its signers by state. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on how each document was drafted, debated and adopted, and explanatory notes on the persons who framed and signed them and the terms of law and government they use. The debates behind the Constitution are No. 12, its defence No. 13, and the case against it No. 14, and Washington’s Farewell Address stands in No. 16, so no document is printed twice in the collection.

title: Notes on the State of Virginia
subtitle: with A Summary View of the Rights of British America and the First Inaugural Address
author: Thomas Jefferson
lead: Thomas Jefferson’s only full-length book, a survey of Virginia written in 1781, with his Summary View of 1774 and his First Inaugural Address of 1801.
description: In 1780 François Barbé-Marbois, secretary of the French legation at Philadelphia, sent a list of questions about their states to members of Congress. Thomas Jefferson, then governor of Virginia, answered his at length, and revised and enlarged the answers into Notes on the State of Virginia. He had it printed privately in Paris in 1785, while he was minister to France, and the London bookseller John Stockdale published the first edition he authorized in 1787. Jefferson was born in 1743 and died on 4 July 1826, fifty years to the day after the Declaration he drafted.

The Notes answer twenty-three queries in turn: Virginia’s boundaries, rivers, mountains, minerals, plants and animals, its peoples, its laws, its constitution, its religion and its manners. In them Jefferson disputes the French naturalist Buffon’s claim that life degenerates in America, argues for religious liberty, proposes a plan of public schools, and writes at length on slavery and on the Native Americans. With them are A Summary View of the Rights of British America (1774), his first public statement of the colonies’ case, and his First Inaugural Address (1801).

No. 10 of Lérins America, in the second part of the collection, the Founding and the Republic, 1771–1799, prints the Notes whole, in the text of the London edition of 1787, with Jefferson’s appendices, and with A Summary View and the First Inaugural Address after it. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the book’s occasion and printing, and explanatory notes on the persons, places, authors and natural history Jefferson names, and on the law and politics of Virginia in his day. His papers of the cabinet years are in No. 15.

title: A Defence of the Constitutions of Government of the United States of America
subtitle: Volume I, with Thoughts on Government
author: John Adams
lead: John Adams’s defence of balanced government, written in London in 1787 while he was the first American minister to Britain, with his Thoughts on Government of 1776.
description: John Adams was born at Braintree, Massachusetts, in 1735, practised law in Boston, and was among the leaders in Congress for independence. He drafted the Massachusetts constitution of 1780, and from 1785 to 1788 he was the first minister of the United States to Britain. In London he read the French statesman Turgot’s criticism of the American states for dividing power among governors, senates and assemblies, and answered it in A Defence of the Constitutions of Government of the United States of America. The first volume appeared early in 1787 and was read in America while the Convention met. Adams was the second President, and died on 4 July 1826.

The Defence argues that liberty is kept only where power is divided among an executive, an upper house and a lower house, each checking the others, and it makes its case by surveying the republics of history, ancient and modern, and the writers on government from Plato to his own century. Volume I, printed here, treats the modern democratic, aristocratic and mixed republics and the philosophers. Before it stands Thoughts on Government (1776), the letter in which Adams first set out the plan many states followed in writing their constitutions.

No. 11 of Lérins America, in the second part of the collection, the Founding and the Republic, 1771–1799, prints Volume I of the Defence whole, in the text of the London edition of 1787, as Adams’s own first volume, with Thoughts on Government before it. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Adams’s life, his mission in London and the reception of the Defence, and explanatory notes on the republics, historians and political writers he surveys, from Plato and Polybius to Machiavelli, Harrington and Turgot, and on the terms of his political science.

title: Notes of Debates in the Federal Convention of 1787
subtitle: with Vices of the Political System of the United States
author: James Madison
lead: James Madison’s daily record of the Constitutional Convention at Philadelphia, from May to September 1787, in two volumes.
description: James Madison was born in Virginia in 1751 and came to the Convention at Philadelphia in May 1787 the best prepared of its delegates. The Convention met in secret, and no official record of its debates was kept beyond a bare journal of motions and votes. Madison took a seat in front of the presiding officer and wrote down the speeches each day, writing them out fully in the evenings. He kept the notes private all his life. They were bought by Congress from his widow and published in 1840, four years after his death.

The Notes follow the Convention from its opening on 25 May to the signing on 17 September: the Virginia Plan and the New Jersey Plan, the dispute between the large states and the small that ended in the Connecticut Compromise, the debates over the executive, the slave trade and the counting of slaves, and the long work of the Committee of Detail and the Committee of Style. At their head stands Madison’s memorandum Vices of the Political System of the United States, written in April 1787. The work is divided at the Convention’s own recess, from 26 July to 6 August.

No. 12 of Lérins America, in the second part of the collection, the Founding and the Republic, 1771–1799, prints the Notes whole in two volumes, divided at the Convention’s recess, from the text of 1840, with the Vices of the Political System at the head of the first. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the Convention, its secrecy and the history of Madison’s record, and explanatory notes on the delegates and their states, the plans and committees, and the history and law the speakers cite. Madison’s papers as Publius are in The Federalist, No. 13.

title: The Federalist
subtitle: The Eighty-Five Papers in Favour of the New Constitution
author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay
lead: The eighty-five papers written under the name Publius in 1787 and 1788 to persuade New York to ratify the Constitution.
description: When the Convention sent the Constitution to the states in September 1787, its ratification in New York was in doubt. Alexander Hamilton, a New York delegate, planned a series of papers in its defence for the city’s newspapers, and enlisted James Madison and John Jay. Writing as Publius, the three published eighty-five papers between October 1787 and August 1788, most of them by Hamilton, many by Madison and five by Jay. The papers were collected in two volumes by J. and A. McLean of New York in 1788, before the series was finished in the newspapers.

The papers argue the insufficiency of the Articles of Confederation, the need for an energetic union, and the plan of the Constitution branch by branch: the extent of the republic and the control of faction (No. 10), the separation of powers and its checks (No. 51), the Senate, the executive and the judiciary, with its power to set aside laws contrary to the Constitution (No. 78). They answer the Constitution’s opponents throughout. All eighty-five are printed here.

No. 13 of Lérins America, in the second part of the collection, the Founding and the Republic, 1771–1799, prints all eighty-five papers whole, in the text of the McLean edition of 1788, with its preface. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the ratification struggle in New York, the three authors and the long question of which wrote the disputed papers, and explanatory notes on the persons, events and opponents the papers name and the history and law they cite. The essays Publius answered are No. 14, and the Convention’s own debates No. 12.

title: Brutus · The Federal Farmer
subtitle: The Anti-Federalist Case, 1787–1788
author: Brutus and the Federal Farmer
lead: The two chief series of essays written against the Constitution in 1787 and 1788, the Anti-Federalist case Publius answered.
description: The Constitution’s opponents, whom its friends named Anti-Federalists, wrote under pseudonyms as its defenders did. The most weighty of their writings were two series. Brutus published sixteen essays in the New-York Journal between October 1787 and April 1788, and the Federal Farmer published a pamphlet of five letters in November 1787 and an Additional Number of thirteen in May 1788. Who wrote them is disputed: Brutus has been ascribed to Robert Yates of New York, and the Farmer to Richard Henry Lee of Virginia or to Melancton Smith of New York, and neither attribution is settled.

Brutus argues that a single republic cannot extend over so large a country without becoming a despotism, that the powers to tax and to make all necessary and proper laws leave the states nothing that cannot be taken, and that the federal judiciary, answerable to no one, will enlarge the national government by construction. The Federal Farmer, more moderate, examines the plan clause by clause and argues for amendments, a bill of rights first among them. Many of the papers of Publius answer their arguments directly.

No. 14 of Lérins America, in the second part of the collection, the Founding and the Republic, 1771–1799, prints both series whole, in the texts of their first printings, Brutus in all sixteen essays and the Federal Farmer in all eighteen letters. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the Anti-Federalists and the ratification debates, giving the attributions as disputed, and explanatory notes on the persons and events the writers name and on each clause of the Constitution they examine. The Federalist, No. 13, is the answering volume.

title: Hamilton and Jefferson on the Constitution
subtitle: The Opinions on the National Bank, the Reports on Public Credit and on Manufactures, and Their Letters
author: Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson
lead: The papers in which Washington’s Secretary of the Treasury and his Secretary of State disputed the meaning of the Constitution, from 1790 to 1793.
description: In Washington’s first administration Alexander Hamilton, at the Treasury, and Thomas Jefferson, at the State Department, came to stand for two readings of the new Constitution and two visions of the republic. Hamilton proposed that the national government assume the states’ war debts, charter a national bank and encourage manufactures. Jefferson held that the government had only the powers the Constitution gave it in words, and feared a moneyed interest tied to the government. Their dispute gave rise to the first American parties.

The volume prints their papers in the order they answered each other: Hamilton’s First Report on the Public Credit (1790), Jefferson’s and Hamilton’s opinions for Washington on the constitutionality of a national bank (February 1791), Hamilton’s Report on Manufactures (1791), and letters of both men to Washington and others on the course of the republic in 1792 and 1793.

No. 15 of Lérins America, in the second part of the collection, the Founding and the Republic, 1771–1799, prints the reports and the opinions on the bank whole, from the texts submitted, with a selection of the two men’s letters. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the first administration and the rise of parties, and explanatory notes on the persons, measures and events the papers name, the economics they assume, and the clauses of the Constitution they dispute. Jefferson’s Notes on the State of Virginia is No. 10, and Hamilton’s papers as Publius are in No. 13.

title: The Farewell Address
subtitle: with the Circular to the States, the Inaugural Addresses and Selected Letters
author: George Washington
lead: George Washington’s address of 1796 on leaving the presidency, with his Newburgh Address, his Circular to the States, his Inaugural Addresses and a selection of his letters.
description: George Washington was born in Virginia in 1732, commanded the Continental Army through the war of independence, presided over the Constitutional Convention and served two terms as the first President. Declining a third, he published his Farewell Address in a Philadelphia newspaper, Claypoole’s American Daily Advertiser, on 19 September 1796. He had drafted it with Hamilton’s help from a draft Madison prepared for him in 1792. He died at Mount Vernon in 1799.

The Farewell Address urges the union of the states, warns against the spirit of party and of faction by region, calls religion and morality indispensable supports of political prosperity, and counsels against permanent alliances with foreign nations. With it are the Newburgh Address (1783), by which he calmed officers of the army threatening Congress, the Circular to the States (1783), his two Inaugural Addresses (1789 and 1793), his letter to the Hebrew Congregation at Newport (1790), and a selection of his letters.

No. 16 of Lérins America, in the second part of the collection, the Founding and the Republic, 1771–1799, prints the Farewell Address and the other addresses whole, from the texts of their first printings, with a selection of Washington’s letters. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Washington’s life and on the making of the Farewell Address, and explanatory notes on the persons and events he names and the occasion of each paper.

title: The Reformed Catholic Reader, Volume I
subtitle: Calvin on the Church, Baptism, and the Supper
author: John Calvin
lead: John Calvin on the Church, on baptism and on the Lord’s Supper, in his own words, the first of three volumes of The Reformed Catholic Reader: Sacramental Calvinism, Calvin, Nevin, and the Confessions.
description: John Calvin was born at Noyon in Picardy in 1509 and trained in law at Orléans and Bourges. Converted to the cause of reform in the early 1530s, he left France and in 1536 published at Basel the first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion. That summer, passing through Geneva, he was kept there by Guillaume Farel. Expelled with Farel in 1538, he spent three years at Strasbourg as minister to its French refugees, beside Martin Bucer, and came back to Geneva in 1541 at the city’s request, with Ecclesiastical Ordinances for its church. He died there in 1564. The volume opens with the life written that year by his successor, Theodore Beza, and with Calvin’s own account of his conversion and calling in the preface to his Commentary on the Psalms (1557).

The rest is arranged as Calvin arranged the fourth book of the Institutes, the Church first, then baptism, then the Supper. On the Church it prints Book IV, chapters 1 to 4, on the Church as the mother of believers, the true Church and the false, the ministry and its calling, and the government of the ancient Church, with his letters to Thomas Cranmer (1552) on a general synod of the Reformed churches and to the King of Poland (1554) on the reform of the Polish church. On baptism it prints chapters 14 to 16, on the sacraments, baptism and infant baptism, with the questions on baptism from the Geneva Catechism and the Genevan form for administering it. On the Supper it prints the Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper (1541), chapter 17, the Catechism’s questions and the Genevan form, and his comment on the tenth and eleventh chapters of First Corinthians. “We are truly made partakers of the proper substance of the body and blood of Jesus Christ,” he writes in the Short Treatise, and in chapter 17 he asks that the Supper be held “at least once a-week.”

No. 1 of Lérins Reformation prints each piece whole within its chapter, letter or office, in the translations of the Calvin Translation Society: the Institutes as Henry Beveridge rendered them in 1845, the treatises, the Catechism and the forms from his Tracts, the commentaries of James Anderson and John Pringle, and the letters as Jules Bonnet edited them. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Calvin’s life, Geneva and the making of these texts, and explanatory notes on the Fathers he cites, the Latin and French behind his key words, and the councils and controversies he answers, with cross-references to the pages of Volume II where Nevin quotes him. The whole Institutes are No. 6. It is the first of the three volumes of The Reformed Catholic Reader, with Nevin’s Mystical Presence in Volume II and the writings of Mercersburg in Volume III.

title: The Reformed Catholic Reader, Volume II
subtitle: Nevin, The Mystical Presence, with the Reformed Confessions
author: John Williamson Nevin
lead: John Williamson Nevin’s Mystical Presence of 1846, his vindication of what he called the Reformed or Calvinistic doctrine of the Holy Eucharist, printed whole with the confessions he cites.
description: John Williamson Nevin was born in 1803 in Franklin County, Pennsylvania, of a Scots-Irish Presbyterian family. He studied at Union College and at Princeton Theological Seminary, where he taught Hebrew for two years in place of Charles Hodge, and from 1830 he taught at the Western Theological Seminary at Allegheny. In 1840 he went to Mercersburg, Pennsylvania, as professor in the theological seminary of the German Reformed Church, and in 1844 he was joined there by the young Swiss historian Philip Schaff. The Mystical Presence appeared at Philadelphia in 1846. Hodge reviewed it in the Biblical Repertory and Princeton Review in 1848, and Nevin answered in the Mercersburg Review in 1850. He died at Lancaster in 1886.

Nevin argues that the Reformed doctrine of the Supper, as Calvin and the early Reformed confessions taught it, was a real communion with the whole person of Christ, “a real communication with his substantial, personal, mediatorial life,” and that much of American Protestantism had left it for a view of the Supper as a memorial alone. His first chapter states the doctrine and gives its historical evidence, from Calvin, the Geneva Catechism and the tract against Hesshusius, through the French, Scots, Belgic and Second Helvetic confessions, the Heidelberg Catechism and Ursinus, to Westminster, Hooker and Owen. The second sets beside it what he calls the modern Puritan theory, the third states the doctrine in his own terms, and the fourth gives the biblical argument, from the Incarnation and the second Adam to the sixth chapter of John. The book opens with his translation of an essay by the German theologian Carl Ullmann on the distinctive character of Christianity.

No. 2 of Lérins Reformation prints The Mystical Presence whole, in the text of the first edition of 1846, with Nevin’s own notes as he left them. After it stands an appendix of the confessions his first chapter examines, their articles on the Church and the sacraments printed whole in the texts of Philip Schaff’s Creeds of Christendom (1877): the French Confession, the Scots Confession, the Belgic Confession, the Second Helvetic Confession and the Westminster Confession. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Nevin’s life, the seminary at Mercersburg and the controversy the book began, and explanatory notes on the Fathers, Reformers and divines he cites, with cross-references to the pages of Volume I where Calvin’s words stand and to the appendix where the confessions’ do. It is the second of the three volumes of The Reformed Catholic Reader, with Calvin in Volume I and the writings of Mercersburg in Volume III.

title: The Reformed Catholic Reader, Volume III
subtitle: Mercersburg on the Church, the Catechism, and the Liturgy
author: John Williamson Nevin and Philip Schaff
lead: The teachers of Mercersburg on the Church, the catechism and the liturgy: Nevin’s Anxious Bench and his history of the Heidelberg Catechism, Schaff’s Principle of Protestantism, and the Order of Worship of 1866.
description: In the 1840s the theological seminary of the German Reformed Church at Mercersburg, Pennsylvania, became the seat of a movement its friends and its critics came to call the Mercersburg theology. Its teachers were John Williamson Nevin, who came there in 1840, and Philip Schaff, born at Chur in Switzerland in 1819 and trained at Tübingen, Halle and Berlin, who arrived in 1844. Against the revival methods spreading through American churches, and against a Protestantism they judged to have forgotten its history, they taught the Church as a living body that grows through the ages, nurtured by its sacraments, its catechism and its worship. Schaff was tried for heresy by his synod in 1845 and acquitted. He later taught at Union Seminary in New York and edited the Creeds of Christendom.

The volume prints four works whole. The Anxious Bench (second edition, 1844) is Nevin’s critique of the anxious bench of the revivals, where seekers were brought forward to be prayed over, setting against what he called the system of the bench the system of the catechism, by which children baptized into the Church are taught and brought to communion. The History and Genius of the Heidelberg Catechism (1847) tells how the catechism of 1563 was made in the Palatinate and what its character is, and the catechism itself follows whole. The Principle of Protestantism (1845), Schaff’s inaugural address, enlarged and translated by Nevin, presents the Reformation as a development within the one Church, not a break from it. Last come the offices of Holy Baptism, the Holy Communion, Confirmation and Ordination from the Order of Worship for the Reformed Church in the United States (1866), the liturgy the movement produced.

No. 3 of Lérins Reformation prints each work whole, in the texts of their first editions, the Heidelberg Catechism in the English of Schaff’s Creeds of Christendom, and the Order of Worship in its edition of 1866. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Mercersburg, its teachers and the controversies they raised, and explanatory notes on the persons, churches and movements they name, the history of the Heidelberg Catechism and of the liturgy, and their sources in the Fathers and the Reformers, with cross-references to the pages of Volumes I and II. It is the last of the three volumes of The Reformed Catholic Reader, with Calvin in Volume I and Nevin’s Mystical Presence in Volume II.

title: The Ninety-Five Theses · The Bondage of the Will
author: Martin Luther
lead: Luther’s theses on indulgences of 1517, which began the Reformation, and his answer to Erasmus on the freedom of the will of 1525, which he counted among the best of his books.
description: Martin Luther was born at Eisleben in 1483, entered the Augustinian friary at Erfurt in 1505 and from 1512 taught Scripture at the young university of Wittenberg. In 1517 the Dominican Johann Tetzel was preaching in the lands near Wittenberg the indulgence granted for the rebuilding of St. Peter’s in Rome, and on 31 October Luther sent Archbishop Albert of Mainz ninety-five theses for a disputation on the power and efficacy of indulgences. They were written in Latin for scholars, but within weeks they were printed and read across Germany, and the controversy that followed led in four years to Luther’s excommunication and his appearance before the Diet of Worms.

Erasmus of Rotterdam, the first scholar of Europe and long a critic of the abuses Luther attacked, would not join him. In September 1524 he published De libero arbitrio, a Diatribe or Discourse on free will, arguing from Scripture and the Fathers that the will has some power to turn toward grace or away from it. Luther answered in December 1525 with De servo arbitrio, The Bondage of the Will, holding that the will fallen from God can do nothing toward its own salvation, and that God’s grace and foreknowledge are the whole ground of it. Erasmus replied at length in the Hyperaspistes of 1526 and 1527. In 1537 Luther wrote to Wolfgang Capito that of all his books he would keep only The Bondage of the Will and the Catechism.

No. 4 of Lérins Reformation, in the collection’s part on the Reformers, 1517–1559, binds the two works whole in the order Luther wrote them: the Theses in the English of the Philadelphia edition of Luther’s Works (1915), and The Bondage of the Will in Henry Cole’s translation of 1823 as revised by Henry Atherton in 1931, with Atherton’s preface. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the indulgence controversy and the debate with Erasmus, and explanatory notes on the persons, places and controversies Luther names and the Scripture, Fathers and schoolmen he cites.

title: Table Talk
subtitle: translated by William Hazlitt
author: Martin Luther
lead: The sayings of Martin Luther at his own table in Wittenberg, written down by his students and guests from about 1531 to 1546, in William Hazlitt’s English of 1857.
description: Martin Luther was born at Eisleben in 1483, entered the Augustinian friary at Erfurt in 1505 and taught theology at Wittenberg from 1512 until his death in 1546. After his marriage to Katharina von Bora in 1525 he lived in the old Augustinian house, the Black Cloister, with his family, students and guests, and at meals he talked freely of everything, from Scripture and doctrine to the papacy, the princes, the devil, music and his own temptations. From about 1531 several of those at table wrote down what he said, among them Veit Dietrich, Johann Mathesius, Anton Lauterbach and Conrad Cordatus. In 1566 Johannes Aurifaber arranged their notes by subject and published them at Eisleben as the Tischreden.

The first English version was made by Captain Henry Bell and published in 1652. In 1857 William Hazlitt revised Bell’s English for Bohn’s Standard Library, keeping Aurifaber’s arrangement by subject, on the Word of God, Christ and the Holy Ghost, sin and free will, the law and the gospel, justification, prayer, the sacraments, the Church, the pope and the councils, the Jews and the Turks, princes and magistrates, marriage, sickness and death, and much else. Some sayings are harsh, on the papacy, on the Jews and on others, and they stand as they were recorded. Because the sayings were noted by others, sometimes years later, the notes give the history of the collections and what may be known of each saying’s source.

No. 5 of Lérins Reformation, in the collection’s part on the Reformers, 1517–1559, prints Hazlitt’s Table Talk whole, as he arranged it, with the matter Hazlitt printed before it. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Luther’s household, the men who took down his words and the history of the text, and explanatory notes on the persons, places and controversies Luther names and the Scripture and Fathers he cites.

title: Institutes of the Christian Religion
subtitle: translated by Henry Beveridge
author: John Calvin
lead: John Calvin’s summary of Christian doctrine in its final form of 1559, in Henry Beveridge’s translation, in four volumes, one to each of Calvin’s four books.
description: Calvin published the first Institutes at Basel in 1536, a small book in six chapters, dedicated to King Francis I of France in defence of the persecuted Protestants of his kingdom. He enlarged it in Latin in 1539, 1543 and 1550, and translated it into French. The final Latin edition of 1559, printed at Geneva, rearranged the whole into four books and eighty chapters, and Calvin said that only then was he satisfied with its order. It became the chief textbook of the Reformed churches. Henry Beveridge translated it for the Calvin Translation Society of Edinburgh in 1845.

The first book treats the knowledge of God the Creator: how God is known in his works and in Scripture, the Trinity, creation and providence. The second treats the knowledge of God the Redeemer in Christ: the fall, the bondage of the will, the law, and the person and offices of the Mediator. The third treats the way in which the grace of Christ is received: faith, repentance, the Christian life, justification, prayer, election, and the resurrection. The fourth treats the outward means by which God draws us into the society of Christ: the Church, its ministry and government, the sacraments, and civil government. Before the whole stand Calvin’s letter to the reader and his address to Francis I.

No. 6 of Lérins Reformation, in the collection’s part on the Reformers, 1517–1559, prints the Institutes whole, in Beveridge’s translation of 1845, in four volumes, each of them one of Calvin’s books, with the prefatory matter in the first and the hundred aphorisms that summarize the work in the fourth. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the making of the Institutes from 1536 to 1559, and explanatory notes on the Fathers, schoolmen and opponents Calvin cites and the Latin of his key terms. The Reformed Catholic Reader, Nos. 1 to 3, prints the chapters on the Church and the sacraments beside the treatises and the liturgy.

title: The Bruised Reed · The Soul’s Conflict
author: Richard Sibbes
lead: Richard Sibbes’s two books of comfort for troubled consciences, The Bruised Reed of 1630 and The Soul’s Conflict with Itself of 1635.
description: Richard Sibbes was born in 1577 at Tostock in Suffolk, the son of a wheelwright, and studied at St John’s College, Cambridge. His preaching at Holy Trinity Church in Cambridge drew the university, and from 1617 he was preacher to the lawyers of Gray’s Inn in London. From 1626 he was also Master of St Catharine’s Hall at Cambridge. He was called the heavenly Doctor Sibbes for the gentleness of his preaching, and he died in 1635. Both books were made from his sermons, The Bruised Reed and Smoking Flax in 1630 and The Soul’s Conflict with Itself in 1635. Richard Baxter said that a copy of The Bruised Reed, bought from a peddler at his father’s door, did much to bring him to faith.

The Bruised Reed expounds the words of Isaiah that Matthew applies to Christ, “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench,” and treats Christ’s tenderness to the weak in faith, the small beginnings of grace, and the way it grows to victory. The Soul’s Conflict takes the psalmist’s question, “Why art thou cast down, O my soul?” (Psalm 42:11), and treats discouragement and melancholy: their causes in the body, the mind and the conscience, the soul’s duty to reason with itself, and its rest in trusting God. Both have been reprinted continually since the seventeenth century.

No. 7 of Lérins Reformation, the first book in the collection’s part on the Puritans, 1630–1684, prints both books whole, in the text of Alexander Grosart’s edition of the Works (1862–1864), with Sibbes’s epistles to the reader. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Sibbes’s life, his preaching and his place among the Puritans, and explanatory notes on the Scripture he expounds, the Fathers and divines he cites, and the words of his English that have changed their sense.

title: The Reformed Pastor
author: Richard Baxter
lead: Richard Baxter’s address of 1656 to the ministers of Worcestershire on the pastor’s work, printed whole, not in the abridgment most editions follow.
description: Richard Baxter was born in Shropshire in 1615, was ordained in the Church of England in 1638, and from 1641 was minister at Kidderminster in Worcestershire, where in the 1650s he and his assistants undertook to teach every family in the parish in turn. In 1652 he drew the ministers of the county into a voluntary association across their differences, and in 1655 they agreed to catechize their parishes as he did. Baxter prepared an address for a day of humiliation they kept at Worcester in December 1655, was kept from giving it by illness, and published it the next year, enlarged, as Gildas Salvianus: The Reformed Pastor. Ejected from the Church of England in 1662, he wrote and preached as a nonconformist until his death in 1691.

The book expounds the charge of Paul to the elders of Ephesus, “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Acts 20:28). Baxter treats first the minister’s care of himself, his own faith, holiness and diligence, then his care of the flock, every member of it, the converted and the unconverted, and the motives to the work. He then argues at length for personal catechizing and instruction, family by family, answers the objections of ministers who thought it beneath them or impossible, and gives directions for doing it. By “reformed” he meant not a party but a pastor renewed in his work.

No. 8 of Lérins Reformation, in the collection’s part on the Puritans, 1630–1684, prints The Reformed Pastor whole, in Baxter’s full text, not the abridgment Samuel Palmer made in 1766, which most later editions follow. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Baxter’s ministry at Kidderminster and the Worcestershire Association, and explanatory notes on the persons, controversies and Church of England practice he names, the Fathers and divines he cites, and the terms of his English.

title: The Mortification of Sin · Of Temptation
author: John Owen
lead: John Owen’s two short treatises on the Christian’s war with sin and temptation, preached to the university at Oxford and published in 1656 and 1658.
description: John Owen was born in 1616 at Stadhampton in Oxfordshire and studied at Queen’s College, Oxford. He became a chaplain to Oliver Cromwell, preached to Parliament, and in 1651 was made Dean of Christ Church, and from 1652 to 1657 Vice-Chancellor of the university. Both treatises were made from sermons he preached at Oxford in those years, to an audience largely of students. After 1660 he led the Congregationalists as a nonconformist in London, and he died in 1683.

Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656) expounds the words of Paul, “if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live” (Romans 8:13). Owen argues that the believer must make it his daily work to put sin to death, that it is done only by the Spirit and through faith in Christ, and he gives particular directions for discerning a sin’s strength and dealing with it. Of Temptation: The Nature and Power of It (1658) expounds the warning of Christ in Gethsemane, “Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation” (Matthew 26:41), and treats what it is to enter into temptation, its seasons and its signs, and the means of keeping from it.

No. 9 of Lérins Reformation, in the collection’s part on the Puritans, 1630–1684, prints both treatises whole, in the text of William Goold’s edition of the Works (1850–1853), with Owen’s prefaces to the reader. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Owen’s years at Oxford and the making of the treatises, and explanatory notes on the Scripture he expounds, the Fathers and divines he cites, and the terms of his English and of his theology.

title: All Things for Good · The Doctrine of Repentance
author: Thomas Watson
lead: Thomas Watson’s exposition of Romans 8:28, first published in 1663 as A Divine Cordial, with his treatise The Doctrine of Repentance of 1668.
description: Thomas Watson was born about 1620 and studied at Emmanuel College, Cambridge. From 1646 he was rector of St Stephen’s, Walbrook, in the City of London, and one of its most popular preachers. A Presbyterian, he was imprisoned briefly in 1651 for his part in a plot to restore Charles II, and in 1662 he was ejected from his living with some two thousand other ministers who would not conform. He preached afterwards in private houses and later in a meeting house at Crosby Hall, and died in 1686. A Divine Cordial, later reprinted under the title by which it is best known, All Things for Good, appeared in 1663, the year after his ejection. The Doctrine of Repentance followed in 1668.

A Divine Cordial expounds the words of Paul, “And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). Watson shows how both the best things, God’s attributes, promises and graces, and the worst things, affliction, temptation, desertion and even sin, are made to work for the good of the godly, and then describes the love of God and the effectual call. The Doctrine of Repentance describes true repentance and its counterfeits, its parts, sight of sin, sorrow, confession, shame, hatred of sin and turning from it, and the motives to it. Both are written in the plain, close and much-quoted style of his sermons.

The title gives A Divine Cordial the name a reader knows it by, and the note on the text gives Watson’s own. title: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
author: John Bunyan
lead: John Bunyan’s own account of his conversion and his call to preach, written in Bedford gaol and published in 1666.
description: John Bunyan was born in 1628 at Elstow, near Bedford, the son of a tinker, and followed his father’s trade. He served in the Parliamentary army as a young man. In the early 1650s, after years of spiritual distress, he joined the separatist congregation at Bedford led by John Gifford and began to preach. In November 1660, after the Restoration, he was arrested for preaching without a licence and spent most of the next twelve years in the county gaol. There he wrote Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, published in 1666. He was released in 1672, became pastor of the Bedford congregation, and died in London in 1688.

The book tells Bunyan’s inward life from his childhood to his imprisonment: the swearing and games of his youth, the bells of Elstow and the game of tipcat on the green, his first reformation, the poor women of Bedford he heard talking of the new birth, and then years of fear that he had sold Christ or committed the unpardonable sin, when texts of Scripture seemed to fight over him, until he found rest in the righteousness of Christ. It closes with his call to the ministry and a short account of his arrest and trial. Bunyan enlarged the book in later editions, and the text printed here is that of the sixth edition of 1688, the last he saw.

No. 11 of Lérins Reformation, in the collection’s part on the Puritans, 1630–1684, prints Grace Abounding whole, in the text of the sixth edition of 1688, with Bunyan’s preface, and the note on the text marks what he added after the first edition. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Bunyan’s life and the Bedford congregation, and explanatory notes on the persons and places he names, the Scripture that fills the book, and the words of his English. title: The Pilgrim’s Progress
subtitle: From This World to That Which Is to Come
author: John Bunyan
lead: John Bunyan’s allegory of the Christian life, both parts whole: Christian’s journey of 1678 and Christiana’s of 1684.
description: Bunyan wrote the first part of The Pilgrim’s Progress, from This World to That Which Is to Come, in Bedford gaol, the den of its first sentence, where “I laid me down in that place to sleep: and as I slept I dreamed a dream.” It was published in London by Nathaniel Ponder in 1678, and Bunyan enlarged it in the editions that followed, the third, of 1679, among them. The second part, telling the journey of Christian’s wife and children, followed in 1684. The book has been translated into some two hundred languages and is among the most widely read books in English.

The first part follows Christian from the City of Destruction, with his burden on his back, through the Slough of Despond and the Wicket Gate, to the cross where the burden falls, then through the Hill Difficulty, the House Beautiful, the fight with Apollyon, the Valley of the Shadow of Death, Vanity Fair where Faithful is put to death, Doubting Castle and Giant Despair, the Delectable Mountains and the river, to the Celestial City. The second part brings Christiana, her four sons and her neighbour Mercy along the same road under the guidance of Mr. Great-heart. Each part opens with a verse apology, and the book is written throughout in the words of the English Bible.

title: Morning and Evening
subtitle: Daily Readings
author: C. H. Spurgeon
lead: C. H. Spurgeon’s readings for every morning and evening of the year, Morning by Morning of 1865 and Evening by Evening of 1868, in two volumes.
description: Charles Haddon Spurgeon was born at Kelvedon in Essex in 1834 and was converted at fifteen in a Primitive Methodist chapel at Colchester. In 1854, aged nineteen, he became pastor of the New Park Street Chapel in London, and his congregation soon outgrew every building, until in 1861 it moved into the Metropolitan Tabernacle, which seated some five thousand. His sermons were printed every week and sold across the world. He read the Puritans all his life and owned a large library of them. He died at Menton in France in 1892. Morning by Morning appeared in 1865 and Evening by Evening in 1868, and his publishers later bound the two together.

Each day of the year has two readings, one for the morning and one for the evening, each a short meditation on a verse of Scripture printed at its head. They range over the whole Bible, from Genesis to Revelation, and over the whole of the Christian life: the person and work of Christ, prayer, assurance, temptation, affliction, the promises, work and rest. Each can be read in a few minutes, at the start and the close of the day, alone or aloud in a household.

No. 13 of Lérins Reformation, the one book in the collection’s last part, the Puritans’ heir, 1865–1868, prints both books whole, in two volumes at Spurgeon’s own division: Morning by Morning in the first and Evening by Evening in the second, each with his preface. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Spurgeon’s life and his debt to the Puritans, a light apparatus of notes on the persons, hymns and allusions the readings assume, and an index of the Scripture they expound.

title: The Elementary Spelling Book
subtitle: The Blue-Backed Speller
author: Noah Webster
lead: Noah Webster’s Blue-Backed Speller, the book from which generations of American children learned to read and spell, in its standard form of 1829, with its fables and woodcuts.
description: Noah Webster was born at West Hartford, Connecticut, in 1758, studied at Yale, and taught school during the war of independence. Dissatisfied with the English spelling books then in use, he published at Hartford in 1783 the first part of A Grammatical Institute of the English Language, a speller meant to give the new nation a uniform American spelling and pronunciation. Renamed The American Spelling Book, it was revised in 1829 as The Elementary Spelling Book, and in that form, bound in its familiar blue covers, it sold in the tens of millions through the nineteenth century and was for many children the only schoolbook they owned. Webster went on to publish his American Dictionary of the English Language in 1828, and died at New Haven in 1843.

The Speller begins with the alphabet and the sounds of the letters, marked by Webster’s own key, and moves by graded tables from words of one syllable to words of five and six, divided and accented for pronunciation. Between the tables stand short reading lessons in plain sentences, many of them moral and religious, and near its end a set of fables with woodcuts, among them the boy who stole apples and the country maid and her milk pail. It closes with tables of words alike in sound and different in sense, of abbreviations, and of numbers.

No. 1 of Lérins Schoolhouse, in the collection’s first part, Reading and spelling, prints the Elementary Spelling Book whole, from its revision of 1829 in the form D. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction for the teacher at home, on the series and how its lessons were used in the one-room school, a guide to Webster’s marks for the sounds of the letters set beside the sounds of present speech, a glossary of words that have dropped out of use, and notes on the fables and lessons.

title: McGuffey’s Eclectic Primer, First and Second Readers

author: William Holmes McGuffey

description: William Holmes McGuffey was born in western Pennsylvania in 1800 and grew up on the Ohio frontier, where he taught in country schools from his early teens. In 1826 he became professor of ancient languages at Miami University in Oxford, Ohio, and in 1833 the Cincinnati publishers Truman and Smith engaged him to compile a series of school readers. The First and Second Readers appeared in 1836 and the Third and Fourth in 1837, and his brother Alexander’s Rhetorical Guide later became the Fifth and Sixth. The Primer begins with the letters and with short words built from them, each lesson headed by a picture and the new words it brings, and ends with simple sentences. The First Reader carries the child through short lessons in print and in script, with the words of each lesson set above it, and the slate exercises that taught writing beside reading. The Second Reader brings longer lessons, stories of children, animals and the farm, short poems, and questions on what has been read, with marks to guide pronunciation. title: Ray’s New Primary Arithmetic · Ray’s New Intellectual Arithmetic
author: Joseph Ray
lead: The first two books of Ray’s New Series, for the youngest pupils, from counting to mental arithmetic with fractions and measures, bound in one volume.
description: Joseph Ray was born in 1807 in Ohio County, Virginia, in what is now West Virginia, and trained as a physician. He turned to teaching, and from 1834 taught mathematics at Woodward College in Cincinnati, of which he became president. His Eclectic Arithmetic, published in 1834 by Truman and Smith, the same firm that published McGuffey’s Readers, grew into a graded series of arithmetics and algebras. Ray died in 1855. His publishers revised the series and issued it as Ray’s New Series in 1877 and 1880, and in that form it was the arithmetic of a large part of the country’s schools for the rest of the century.

The New Primary Arithmetic teaches the youngest pupils to count, read and write numbers, and to add, subtract, multiply and divide, by lessons built on pictures and objects and on simple questions about the things of a child’s day. The New Intellectual Arithmetic carries the same pupils into mental arithmetic, in the tradition the American teacher Warren Colburn began in 1821: problems worked in the head and explained aloud, through the four rules, fractions, and the measures of money, length, weight and time, before the pupil writes figures on a slate.
