title: The Iliad
author: Homer
lead: Homer’s poem of the wrath of Achilles in the tenth year of the war at Troy, in Samuel Butler’s English prose.
description: The Iliad is the oldest work of Greek literature and stands at the head of the literature of Europe. The Greeks ascribed it to Homer, a poet of whose life nothing certain is known, and it seems to have taken its present form in the eighth or seventh century before Christ, at the end of a long tradition of poetry sung without writing. It was learned by heart in the schools of Greece for a thousand years, and every later epic of the West, from Virgil’s to Milton’s, was written in answer to it.

Its twenty-four books cover some fifty days in the tenth year of the Greek siege of Troy. Achilles, slighted by Agamemnon, withdraws from the fighting, and the Trojans under Hector drive the Greeks back to their ships. Only the death of his friend Patroclus brings Achilles back to the field. He kills Hector and drags his body before the walls, and the poem ends when the old king Priam comes by night to his tent to ransom his son.

No. 1 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s first part, The ancients, prints the Iliad whole in the English prose of Samuel Butler (1898). The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the poem, its making and its readers, and explanatory notes on the gods and heroes, the places of the Greek world, and the customs of war and hospitality the poem takes for granted.

title: The Odyssey
author: Homer
lead: Homer’s poem of the ten years’ homecoming of Odysseus from Troy to Ithaca, in Samuel Butler’s English prose.
description: The Odyssey, the second of the two poems the Greeks ascribed to Homer, was composed like the Iliad near the end of a long tradition of oral poetry, probably a little after it. Where the Iliad is a poem of war, the Odyssey is a poem of wandering and return. Its hero, Odysseus of Ithaca, the cleverest of the Greeks at Troy, became for later ages the figure of the traveller and of the man who endures.

The poem opens on Ithaca in the tenth year after the fall of Troy, where Odysseus’ wife Penelope is besieged by suitors and his son Telemachus sets out to seek news of him. Odysseus himself tells the tale of his wanderings at the court of the Phaeacians: the Lotus-eaters, the Cyclops, Circe, the visit to the dead, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis. The second half brings him home in disguise to test his household and to reckon with the suitors.

No. 2 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s first part, The ancients, prints the Odyssey whole in the English prose of Samuel Butler (1900). The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the poem and its place beside the Iliad, and explanatory notes on its gods and peoples, its geography, real and imagined, and the customs of the Greek household.

title: The Republic
author: Plato
lead: Plato’s dialogue on justice, the soul and the city, in Benjamin Jowett’s translation.
description: Plato was born at Athens about 428 BC, of a noble family, and became as a young man a follower of Socrates. After Socrates was condemned to death by the Athenians in 399 he left the city for some years, and on his return founded the Academy, the school where Aristotle studied for twenty years. He wrote dialogues for some fifty years, in nearly all of which Socrates is the chief speaker. The Republic, written about 375 BC, is the most read of them.

It begins with a question put at a gathering in the Piraeus: what is justice, and is the just man happier than the unjust? To answer it Socrates builds a city in words, with its guardians, its education in music and gymnastic, and its philosopher kings, and finds in it the image of the soul and its three parts. On the way come the allegory of the cave, the divided line and the quarrel with the poets, and at the close the myth of Er, a soldier who returned from the dead to tell of the judgment of souls.

No. 3 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s first part, The ancients, prints the Republic whole, all ten books, in the translation of Benjamin Jowett, Master of Balliol College, Oxford, from his third edition of 1892. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Plato, Socrates and the Athens of their day, and explanatory notes on the persons of the dialogue, the poets and myths it quotes, and the terms of Greek philosophy.

title: Meditations
author: Marcus Aurelius
lead: The private notebooks of the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, written on campaign, in George Long’s translation.
description: Marcus Aurelius was born at Rome in AD 121, adopted into the imperial family as a boy, and reigned as emperor from 161 until his death in 180. He was trained in the Stoic philosophy of Epictetus and his school, and much of his reign was spent on the northern frontier, in wars against the Germanic peoples along the Danube. The twelve books known as the Meditations were written in Greek in those years, for himself alone. The oldest manuscripts call them To Himself.

They are not a treatise but a notebook: reminders, maxims and short reflections on duty and death, the order of nature and the shortness of life, on bearing with other men and doing the work of the day without complaint. The first book is a list of what he learned from his family and teachers. The rest returns again and again to a few Stoic convictions, set down as a man sets them down who needs them.

No. 4 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s first part, The ancients, prints the Meditations whole in the translation of George Long (1862), long the standard English version. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Marcus, his reign and the Stoic school, and explanatory notes on the persons he names, his Stoic terms and the authors he quotes.

title: The Divine Comedy
author: Dante Alighieri
lead: Dante’s journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, in Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s translation, in three volumes.
description: Dante Alighieri was born at Florence in 1265 and took part in the government of his city until 1302, when the faction opposed to his own came to power and he was exiled under sentence of death. He never returned. He wrote the Commedia in the years of his exile, in the Tuscan of his own speech rather than in Latin, and finished it shortly before his death at Ravenna in 1321. Later readers added the word Divine to its title.

The poem tells of a journey made in Holy Week of the year 1300. Lost in a dark wood, Dante is led by the poet Virgil down through the nine circles of Hell and up the mountain of Purgatory, and then by Beatrice, the Florentine woman he had loved in his youth, through the heavens to the vision of God. Its hundred cantos, in the interlocking rhyme Dante invented for it, gather the learning of the Middle Ages, its theology, its astronomy and its politics, into one story.

No. 5 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s second part, The Middle Ages and the Renaissance, prints the Comedy whole in the line-for-line translation of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1867), in three volumes, Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso, with Longfellow’s own notes. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Dante, Florence and the making of the poem, and explanatory notes on the persons Dante meets, the history of the Italian cities, and the theology and astronomy of his journey.

title: The Canterbury Tales
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
lead: Geoffrey Chaucer’s tales of the pilgrims on the road to Canterbury, in his own Middle English, glossed.
description: Geoffrey Chaucer was born in London about 1343, the son of a wine merchant, and spent his life in the service of the English court as a soldier, envoy, customs officer and clerk of the king’s works. He travelled to France and Italy on the king’s business, read Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio, and was the first great poet to write in English. He worked on the Canterbury Tales from about 1387 until his death in 1400, and left them unfinished.

In the General Prologue some thirty pilgrims meet at the Tabard Inn in Southwark on their way to the shrine of St Thomas Becket at Canterbury, and agree to tell tales on the road. They are a cross-section of England, from the Knight to the Miller, the Prioress to the Pardoner, the Wife of Bath to the poor Parson. Their tales are of every kind the Middle Ages knew: romance, fabliau, saint’s life, sermon, fable and beast tale.

No. 6 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s second part, The Middle Ages and the Renaissance, prints the Tales whole in Chaucer’s own Middle English, from the text of Walter W. Skeat, with the hard words glossed on the page. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Chaucer, his England and the pilgrimage, a guide to reading his English aloud, and explanatory notes on the pilgrims’ trades, the Church of his day, and the books and stories he drew on.

title: The Prince
author: Niccolò Machiavelli
lead: Machiavelli’s handbook for a new prince, the founding book of modern political thought, in W. K. Marriott’s translation.
description: Niccolò Machiavelli was born at Florence in 1469 and served the Florentine republic for fourteen years as secretary to its council of war and as its envoy to France, to the Emperor and to Cesare Borgia. When the Medici returned to power in 1512 he lost his post, was imprisoned and tortured, and retired to a farm outside the city. There, in 1513, he wrote The Prince, dedicated to Lorenzo de’ Medici. It was printed in 1532, five years after his death.

In twenty-six short chapters he sets out how principalities are won and how they are kept: by arms, by fortune, by crime or by the favour of the people. He writes of mercenaries and citizen armies, of whether a prince should be loved or feared, of keeping faith, and of fortune, which he likens to a river in flood. The last chapter is a call to free Italy from the foreign armies that had overrun it.

No. 7 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s second part, The Middle Ages and the Renaissance, prints The Prince whole in the translation of W. K. Marriott (1908). The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Machiavelli, the Florence of the Medici and the Italian wars, and explanatory notes on the popes, princes and captains he names and the ancient histories he takes his examples from.

title: Hamlet · Othello · King Lear · Macbeth
subtitle: The Major Plays of Shakespeare, Volume I: The Great Tragedies
author: William Shakespeare
lead: Shakespeare’s four great tragedies, written between about 1600 and 1606, each play whole.
description: William Shakespeare was born at Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564 and by the early 1590s was in London as an actor and playwright. He became a sharer in the Lord Chamberlain’s Men, later the King’s Men, the leading company of the day, and wrote for it some thirty-seven plays, many for the Globe theatre on the south bank of the Thames. He retired to Stratford and died there in 1616. His plays were gathered by two of his fellow actors in the First Folio of 1623.

The four tragedies in this volume were written in the first years of the seventeenth century: Hamlet, the prince of Denmark charged by his father’s ghost with revenge, Othello, the Moorish general destroyed by his ensign’s lies, King Lear, the old king who divides his kingdom among his daughters, and Macbeth, the Scottish thane who murders his king. They have been taken since the eighteenth century as the summit of his work.

No. 8 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s second part, The Middle Ages and the Renaissance, the first of three volumes of Shakespeare’s major plays, prints the four tragedies whole, from the Globe text of W. G. Clark and W. Aldis Wright. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Shakespeare, his theatre and the tragedies, notes on the page for words and usages that have changed since his day, and explanatory notes on the history, law and belief behind the plays.

title: Romeo and Juliet · Julius Caesar · The Merchant of Venice
subtitle: The Major Plays of Shakespeare, Volume II
author: William Shakespeare
lead: Three plays of Shakespeare’s middle years, a tragedy of love, a tragedy of Rome and a comedy of Venice, each whole.
description: The three plays in this volume belong to the years 1595 to 1599, when Shakespeare’s company was the Lord Chamberlain’s Men and the Globe was built on the Bankside. Romeo and Juliet was among his first great successes. The Merchant of Venice followed about 1596, and Julius Caesar was perhaps the first play acted at the new Globe, in 1599.

Romeo and Juliet is the story of two young lovers of Verona whose families are at feud. Julius Caesar, drawn from Plutarch’s Lives, follows the conspiracy of Brutus and Cassius, the murder in the Capitol and the civil war that came after. The Merchant of Venice sets the merchant Antonio, who borrows on the security of a pound of his own flesh, against the moneylender Shylock, and ends at Belmont with Portia’s caskets and rings.

No. 9 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s second part, The Middle Ages and the Renaissance, the second of three volumes of Shakespeare’s major plays, prints the three plays whole, from the Globe text of W. G. Clark and W. Aldis Wright. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the plays and their Italian and Roman sources, notes on the page for words and usages that have changed since Shakespeare’s day, and explanatory notes on the history and customs behind them.

title: A Midsummer Night’s Dream · Twelfth Night · Much Ado About Nothing · The Tempest
subtitle: The Major Plays of Shakespeare, Volume III: The Comedies
author: William Shakespeare
lead: Four of Shakespeare’s comedies, from the Athenian wood of A Midsummer Night’s Dream to Prospero’s island in The Tempest, each whole.
description: Shakespeare wrote comedies through all his career. A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Much Ado About Nothing belong to the later 1590s, Twelfth Night to about 1601, and The Tempest, the last play he wrote alone, to 1611. They were among the most popular of his plays in his own lifetime and have held the stage ever since.

In A Midsummer Night’s Dream four young lovers and a company of Athenian workmen lose their way in a wood ruled by the fairy king and queen. Much Ado About Nothing sets the sparring of Beatrice and Benedick beside a plot against a bride. Twelfth Night follows the shipwrecked Viola, disguised as a boy, through the households of Illyria. In The Tempest the exiled Duke Prospero, a magician, brings his enemies to his island by a storm and at the end forgives them and gives up his art.

No. 10 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s second part, The Middle Ages and the Renaissance, the last of three volumes of Shakespeare’s major plays, prints the four comedies whole, from the Globe text of W. G. Clark and W. Aldis Wright. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Shakespeare’s comedy and its sources, notes on the page for words and usages that have changed since his day, and explanatory notes on the songs, customs and beliefs the plays take for granted.

title: Don Quixote
author: Miguel de Cervantes
lead: Cervantes’s story of the knight of La Mancha and his squire Sancho Panza, both parts whole, in John Ormsby’s translation, in two volumes.
description: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra was born at Alcalá de Henares in 1547. He was wounded at the battle of Lepanto, losing the use of his left hand, was captured by Barbary corsairs and spent five years a captive in Algiers, and later worked as a commissary and tax collector in Andalusia and was jailed over his accounts. The first part of Don Quixote appeared at Madrid in 1605 and was an immediate success. The second followed in 1615, the year before his death.

An old gentleman of La Mancha, his wits turned by reading romances of chivalry, takes the name Don Quixote, puts on his great-grandfather’s armour and rides out with a farm labourer, Sancho Panza, as his squire, to right the wrongs of the world. He takes windmills for giants and inns for castles. In the second part the pair meet people who have read the first, and the book becomes a book about itself. It is often called the first modern novel.

No. 11 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s second part, The Middle Ages and the Renaissance, prints Don Quixote whole in two volumes, Cervantes’s own two parts of 1605 and 1615, in the translation of John Ormsby (1885). The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Cervantes and the Spain of Philip II and Philip III, and explanatory notes on the romances of chivalry, the proverbs Sancho strings together, and the places, customs and coins of the Spain the knight rides through.

title: Paradise Lost
author: John Milton
lead: Milton’s epic of the fall of the angels and of man, in the twelve-book text of 1674.
description: John Milton was born in London in 1608 and educated at St Paul’s School and Christ’s College, Cambridge. He gave twenty years of his life to prose in the cause of Parliament and the Commonwealth, served Cromwell’s government as its Latin secretary, and lost his sight in its service. At the Restoration of Charles II he was briefly imprisoned. Blind, he dictated Paradise Lost, which was published in ten books in 1667 and in twelve in 1674, the year of his death.

The poem begins in Hell, where Satan and the rebel angels lie on a burning lake after their fall from Heaven, and follows Satan’s journey to the new world God has made and to the garden where Adam and Eve live in innocence. The archangel Raphael tells Adam of the war in Heaven and of the Creation. Eve is tempted and eats of the forbidden tree, Adam eats with her, and the archangel Michael shows Adam the history of the world to come before the two are led out of Eden.

No. 12 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s third part, From Milton to the Romantics, prints Paradise Lost whole in the twelve books of the second edition of 1674, with Milton’s own Arguments and his note on the verse. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Milton, the English Revolution and the making of the poem, and explanatory notes on its biblical sources, its classical allusions, its theology and the astronomy of its universe.

title: Gulliver’s Travels
subtitle: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World
author: Jonathan Swift
lead: Jonathan Swift’s four voyages of Lemuel Gulliver, ship’s surgeon, to Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa and the land of the Houyhnhnms.
description: Jonathan Swift was born at Dublin in 1667 of English parents, was ordained in the Church of Ireland, and in 1713 became Dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin, where he remained until his death in 1745. He was the foremost satirist of his age and a pamphleteer for the Tory ministry of Queen Anne. Gulliver’s Travels was published anonymously in London in 1726, and was read, the poet John Gay wrote to him, from the cabinet council to the nursery.

Lemuel Gulliver, a ship’s surgeon, tells of four voyages. In Lilliput he is a giant among people six inches high, and in Brobdingnag a manikin among giants. The third voyage takes him to the flying island of Laputa and its projectors, and to the immortal Struldbrugs. In the fourth he comes to a land ruled by rational horses, the Houyhnhnms, where human beings, the Yahoos, are brute beasts, and he returns home unable to bear the company of his own kind.

No. 13 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s third part, From Milton to the Romantics, prints the Travels whole, from George Faulkner’s Dublin edition of 1735, which Swift revised. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Swift, the politics of his day and the book’s reception, and explanatory notes on its targets in the court, the Royal Society and the parties of the reigns of Queen Anne and George I.

title: Sense and Sensibility
author: Jane Austen
lead: Jane Austen’s first novel, of the sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, published in 1811.
description: Jane Austen was born in 1775 at Steventon in Hampshire, where her father was rector, the seventh of eight children. She wrote from girlhood, and in the 1790s drafted the novels that became Sense and Sensibility and Pride and Prejudice. Sense and Sensibility, her first book, was published in 1811 at her own risk, with the description By a Lady on its title page. Its success, modest as it was, opened the way for the others.

On their father’s death the Dashwood sisters, with their mother and younger sister, are left with little money and move to a cottage in Devonshire. Elinor, the elder, keeps her feelings to herself and her conduct governed by judgment. Marianne, the younger, gives herself wholly to her feelings and to the dashing John Willoughby. Both are disappointed in love, and the novel follows how each bears it.

No. 14 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s third part, From Milton to the Romantics, the first of the press’s five volumes of Austen’s novels, prints Sense and Sensibility whole, from the second edition of 1813, the last Austen revised. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Austen, her family and the England of the Regency, and explanatory notes on its money, inheritance and manners, and the words whose sense has moved since her day.

title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
lead: Jane Austen’s novel of Elizabeth Bennet and Mr Darcy, published in 1813.
description: Pride and Prejudice was first drafted in 1796 and 1797, when Jane Austen was in her early twenties, under the title First Impressions. Her father offered it to a London publisher, who declined it unseen. Revised and given its present title, it was published in January 1813 by Thomas Egerton, the publisher of Sense and Sensibility, and Austen called it her own darling child. It has been the best loved of her novels ever since.

Mr and Mrs Bennet of Longbourn have five daughters and no son, and their estate is entailed away to a cousin. When the rich and amiable Mr Bingley takes a house nearby, he brings his friend Mr Darcy, whose pride offends the second daughter, Elizabeth, at their first meeting. The novel follows how her prejudice and his pride are undone, through his first proposal and her refusal, his letter, her visit to Pemberley, and her sister Lydia’s elopement.

No. 15 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s third part, From Milton to the Romantics, prints Pride and Prejudice whole, from the first edition of 1813. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the novel’s making and its reception, and explanatory notes on the entail, the militia, the clergy and their livings, the conduct of a Regency courtship, and the words whose sense has changed since Austen’s day.

title: Mansfield Park
author: Jane Austen
lead: Jane Austen’s novel of Fanny Price, a poor relation raised at Mansfield Park, published in 1814.
description: Mansfield Park was the first novel Jane Austen wrote in her maturity, begun in 1811 at Chawton in Hampshire, where she had settled with her mother and sister in a cottage on her brother Edward’s estate. It was published in 1814, sold out its first edition in six months, and brought her more money than either of the books before it. It is the most serious of her novels and the one in which she writes most directly of ordination and the duties of a clergyman.

Fanny Price, the daughter of a poor family in Portsmouth, is taken at ten to live with her rich uncle and aunt, Sir Thomas and Lady Bertram, at Mansfield Park in Northamptonshire. Timid and overlooked, she grows up beside her four cousins and loves the younger son, Edmund, who means to be a clergyman. While Sir Thomas is away on his estates in Antigua, the arrival of the worldly Henry and Mary Crawford, and a plan to stage a play, unsettle the house.

No. 16 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s third part, From Milton to the Romantics, prints Mansfield Park whole, from the second edition of 1816, which Austen corrected. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the novel and its time, and explanatory notes on the Navy, the West India estates and the slave trade the novel touches on, the private theatricals, the clergy, and the words whose sense has moved since Austen’s day.

title: Emma
author: Jane Austen
lead: Jane Austen’s comedy of Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever and rich, published in 1815.
description: Emma was written at Chawton in 1814 and 1815 and published by John Murray in December 1815, dedicated at his request to the Prince Regent, who admired her novels. Jane Austen said before she began it that she was going to take a heroine whom no one but herself would much like. It is the longest of her novels and the one most admired for its art.

Emma Woodhouse, twenty-one, lives with her anxious father at Hartfield in the village of Highbury and, believing herself a judge of hearts, sets out to arrange the marriages of her neighbours, beginning with her young friend Harriet Smith. Her schemes go wrong one after another. Mr Knightley, an old friend of the family, is the one person who tells her when she is wrong.

No. 17 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s third part, From Milton to the Romantics, prints Emma whole, from the first edition of 1815. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the novel and its reception, and explanatory notes on the ranks of a country village, its farming and its visiting, and the words whose sense has moved since Austen’s day.

title: Northanger Abbey · Persuasion
author: Jane Austen
lead: Jane Austen’s comedy of a young reader of Gothic novels and her last finished novel, published together after her death in 1817.
description: Jane Austen died at Winchester in July 1817, at the age of forty-one. In December of that year her brother Henry published together the two novels she had left: Northanger Abbey, written in the late 1790s and sold in 1803 to a publisher who never printed it, and Persuasion, finished in 1816. Henry’s biographical notice, printed at their head, was the first time the public was told her name.

Northanger Abbey follows Catherine Morland, a young reader of Gothic novels, on her first visit to Bath and then to the abbey of the Tilney family, where she imagines dark secrets. Persuasion is the story of Anne Elliot, who at nineteen was persuaded to break her engagement to a young naval officer without fortune, Frederick Wentworth, and who meets him again eight years later, now a rich captain, in Somerset and at Bath.

No. 18 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s third part, From Milton to the Romantics, prints the two novels whole, as they were first published together, with Henry Austen’s Biographical Notice of the Author. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the last years of Austen’s life, and explanatory notes on the Navy after the wars with France, Bath and its society, the Gothic novels Catherine reads, and the words whose sense has moved.

title: Frankenstein
subtitle: or, The Modern Prometheus
author: Mary Shelley
lead: Mary Shelley’s novel of the student who makes a living man, in its first text of 1818.
description: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in London in 1797, the daughter of the philosopher William Godwin and of Mary Wollstonecraft, who died days after her birth. At sixteen she left England with the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, whom she married in 1816. That summer, beside Lake Geneva in the company of Lord Byron, a contest to write ghost stories gave her the idea for Frankenstein. It was published anonymously in three volumes in January 1818, when she was twenty.

In letters home, an English explorer in the Arctic tells of a stranger he has taken aboard his ship. The stranger is Victor Frankenstein of Geneva, who as a student at Ingolstadt discovered how to give life to dead matter, made a man, and abandoned the creature in horror. The creature tells his own story, of how he learned to speak and read and was driven off by everyone he met, and of his revenge on his maker.

No. 19 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s third part, From Milton to the Romantics, prints Frankenstein whole in its first text of 1818. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Mary Shelley, her circle and the summer of 1816, and explanatory notes on the science of galvanism and anatomy the novel draws on, the books the creature reads, and the places of the story.

title: A Christmas Carol · The Chimes · The Cricket on the Hearth
author: Charles Dickens
lead: Dickens’s first three Christmas books, of 1843, 1844 and 1845, A Christmas Carol and the two that followed it.
description: Charles Dickens was born at Portsmouth in 1812 and knew poverty as a child, when his father was imprisoned for debt and the boy was sent to work in a blacking factory. By 1843 he was the most popular novelist in England. A Christmas Carol, written in six weeks that autumn and published on 19 December, sold six thousand copies by Christmas Eve, and for the next Christmases he wrote a short book for each.

In A Christmas Carol the miser Ebenezer Scrooge is visited on Christmas Eve by the ghost of his partner Marley and by three spirits, of Christmas past, present and yet to come. The Chimes, a story for New Year’s Eve, takes a poor ticket-porter, Trotty Veck, through a vision shown him by the spirits of the church bells. The Cricket on the Hearth is a fireside tale of the carrier John Peerybingle, his young wife and a mysterious lodger.

No. 20 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s fourth part, The nineteenth-century novel, prints the three books whole, from Dickens’s first editions, with John Leech’s illustrations to the Carol. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Dickens, the London of the hungry forties and the keeping of Christmas, and explanatory notes on its money, food and customs, and the poor laws and politics Dickens had in mind.

title: Jane Eyre
subtitle: An Autobiography
author: Charlotte Brontë
lead: Charlotte Brontë’s novel of the orphan governess Jane Eyre and Mr Rochester of Thornfield Hall, published in 1847.
description: Charlotte Brontë was born in 1816 at Thornton in Yorkshire, the third of six children of Patrick Brontë, an Irish-born clergyman who became perpetual curate of Haworth on the moors. Her mother and two elder sisters died when she was a child. She worked as a teacher and governess and studied at Brussels, and with her sisters Emily and Anne published a book of poems in 1846 under the names Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell. Jane Eyre, published as Currer Bell’s in October 1847, was an immediate success.

Jane Eyre, an orphan, tells her own story: her unhappy childhood in her aunt’s house, her years at the charity school of Lowood, and her post as governess at Thornfield Hall, where she and its master, Edward Rochester, fall in love. On their wedding day a secret of the house comes to light, and Jane leaves Thornfield with nothing. The novel follows her to the moors, to a proposal from the clergyman St John Rivers, and back.

No. 21 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s fourth part, The nineteenth-century novel, prints Jane Eyre whole, from the third edition of 1848, the last Charlotte Brontë saw through the press. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on the Brontës and Haworth, and explanatory notes on the schools and the work of a governess, the law of marriage in her day, and the books and Scriptures Jane quotes.

title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë
lead: Emily Brontë’s only novel, of Heathcliff and Catherine Earnshaw on the Yorkshire moors, published in 1847.
description: Emily Brontë was born at Thornton in Yorkshire in 1818 and grew up at the parsonage of Haworth with her sisters Charlotte and Anne and her brother Branwell. Apart from a few months at school and at Brussels she spent almost all her life there, and those who knew her remembered her as reserved and devoted to the moors. Wuthering Heights was published under the name Ellis Bell in December 1847. She died of consumption a year later, at thirty.

Mr Lockwood, the new tenant of Thrushcross Grange, visits his landlord Heathcliff at the farmhouse of Wuthering Heights and hears from the housekeeper, Nelly Dean, the history of the two houses. Heathcliff, a foundling brought home by old Mr Earnshaw, grows up with the daughter of the house, Catherine. When she marries Edgar Linton of the Grange, Heathcliff sets out to take his revenge on both families, into the second generation.

No. 22 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s fourth part, The nineteenth-century novel, prints Wuthering Heights whole, from the first edition of 1847, with Charlotte Brontë’s Biographical Notice of her sisters. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Emily Brontë and Haworth, and explanatory notes on the Yorkshire speech of the servant Joseph, the law of inheritance the plot turns on, and the farming life of the moors.

title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
lead: Nathaniel Hawthorne’s novel of Hester Prynne in Puritan Boston, published in 1850.
description: Nathaniel Hawthorne was born at Salem, Massachusetts, in 1804, the descendant of Puritan magistrates, one of whom had been a judge at the Salem witch trials. After college at Bowdoin he spent years writing tales in obscurity, and in 1846 he was appointed surveyor of the Salem custom house. Dismissed when the administration changed in 1849, he wrote The Scarlet Letter, which was published at Boston in 1850 and made his name.

In the Boston of the 1640s, Hester Prynne, whose husband has not come from England, is made to stand on the scaffold with her infant daughter Pearl and to wear on her breast a scarlet A for adultery. She will not name the child’s father. Her husband arrives that day under another name and sets himself to find the man, who is the young minister Arthur Dimmesdale, revered by his congregation and hiding his sin. The book opens with Hawthorne’s sketch The Custom-House.

No. 23 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s fourth part, The nineteenth-century novel, prints The Scarlet Letter whole, with The Custom-House, from the second edition of 1850. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Hawthorne and the New England of his fathers, and explanatory notes on the Puritan colony, its government and its churches, its laws and punishments, and the persons from its history who appear in the story.

title: Moby-Dick
subtitle: or, The Whale
author: Herman Melville
lead: Herman Melville’s novel of Captain Ahab’s hunt for the white whale, published in 1851.
description: Herman Melville was born in New York in 1819. After his father’s ruin and death he went to sea, and in 1841 sailed from Fairhaven on the whaler Acushnet, deserted in the Marquesas, and came home by way of Tahiti and Hawaii in a frigate of the United States Navy. His first books, Typee and Omoo, drawn from those years, made him famous. Moby-Dick, published in London and New York in 1851, sold poorly in his lifetime, and he died in 1891 nearly forgotten. It is now counted among the greatest American novels.

Its narrator, who asks to be called Ishmael, ships from Nantucket on the whaler Pequod with the harpooner Queequeg. Once at sea the captain, Ahab, who lost his leg to a great white sperm whale, tells the crew that the voyage is to hunt that one whale round the world. The story of the hunt is set among chapters on whales and whaling, sermons, soliloquies and scenes written like a play.

No. 24 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s fourth part, The nineteenth-century novel, prints Moby-Dick whole, from the first American edition of 1851, with its Etymology and Extracts. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Melville and the American whale fishery, and explanatory notes on ships and whaling, the Bible and the books Melville quotes, and the nautical words of the story.

title: Walden · Civil Disobedience
author: Henry David Thoreau
lead: Thoreau’s account of two years in a cabin by Walden Pond, with his essay on resistance to civil government.
description: Henry David Thoreau was born at Concord, Massachusetts, in 1817 and lived nearly all his life there. A graduate of Harvard, he worked as a schoolteacher, surveyor and pencil maker, and was a friend of Ralph Waldo Emerson and for a time a member of his household. From July 1845 to September 1847 he lived in a cabin he built himself on Emerson’s land by Walden Pond. Walden, rewritten over several years from his journals, was published in 1854. He died at Concord in 1862.

Walden tells of the building of the cabin, the bean field, the pond in every season, the animals and the visitors, and of what Thoreau thought a man needs to live, set against the quiet desperation he saw in the lives of his neighbours. Resistance to Civil Government, later called Civil Disobedience, published in 1849, was written after he spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax to a government that upheld slavery and made war on Mexico.

No. 25 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s fourth part, The nineteenth-century novel, prints Walden whole, from the first edition of 1854, and Civil Disobedience after it, from its first printing of 1849. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Thoreau and the Concord of the Transcendentalists, and explanatory notes on its plants and animals, the classics and Eastern scriptures he quotes, and the politics of slavery and the Mexican War.

title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens
lead: Dickens’s novel of the orphan Pip, the convict on the marshes and the great expectations that come to him, published in 1861.
description: Great Expectations was Charles Dickens’s thirteenth novel, published in weekly parts in his own magazine, All the Year Round, from December 1860 to August 1861, and as a book in 1861. Dickens, then nearly fifty and the most famous writer in the English-speaking world, set it partly in the Kentish marshes near Rochester, the country of his own childhood. It is told in the first person, as David Copperfield had been, and many have counted it his finest novel.

Philip Pirrip, called Pip, an orphan raised by his sister and her husband Joe Gargery, the blacksmith, meets an escaped convict in the churchyard on the marshes and helps him. He is taken to play at the house of Miss Havisham, a rich woman jilted on her wedding day, and falls in love with her ward, Estella. When an unknown benefactor gives him the great expectations of a gentleman, Pip leaves the forge for London and learns to be ashamed of Joe.

No. 26 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s fourth part, The nineteenth-century novel, prints Great Expectations whole, from the first edition of 1861. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Dickens in the 1860s and the novel’s serial publication, with the ending he first wrote and then changed, and explanatory notes on the law and the prisons, transportation to Australia, the Inns of Court, and the money of the story.

title: Crime and Punishment
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
lead: Dostoevsky’s novel of the student Raskolnikov, who kills a pawnbroker in St Petersburg, in Constance Garnett’s translation.
description: Fyodor Dostoevsky was born at Moscow in 1821, the son of a doctor. His first novel, Poor Folk, made him famous at twenty-four. In 1849 he was arrested with the members of a socialist circle, condemned to death and reprieved on the scaffold, and he served four years at hard labour in Siberia and five more as a soldier. Crime and Punishment, written under the pressure of debts and published in the Russian Messenger through 1866, was the first of the great novels of his last fifteen years.

Rodion Raskolnikov, a poor former student in St Petersburg, persuades himself that an extraordinary man may step over the moral law, and murders an old pawnbroker with an axe. The novel follows him through the days after the crime: his fever, his mother and sister, the drunken clerk Marmeladov and his daughter Sonia, who has gone on the streets to feed her family, and the patient examining magistrate Porfiry, until he confesses and goes to Siberia, with Sonia following.

No. 27 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s fourth part, The nineteenth-century novel, prints Crime and Punishment whole in the translation of Constance Garnett (1914). The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Dostoevsky and the Russia of the 1860s, and explanatory notes on the city and its streets, Russian names and forms of address, ranks and money, the Gospel of the raising of Lazarus that Sonia reads, and the ideas of the day the novel argues with.

title: Anna Karenina
author: Leo Tolstoy
lead: Tolstoy’s novel of Anna Karenina and of Konstantin Levin, in Constance Garnett’s translation, in two volumes.
description: Count Leo Tolstoy was born in 1828 at Yasnaya Polyana, his family’s estate south of Moscow, served as an artillery officer in the Caucasus and at the siege of Sevastopol, and returned to his estate to farm, to teach the peasant children and to write. After War and Peace he began Anna Karenina in 1873, and it appeared in parts in the Russian Messenger from 1875 to 1877 and as a book in 1878. Soon after finishing it Tolstoy passed through the religious crisis he described in his Confession.

Anna Karenina, the wife of a high official in St Petersburg, falls in love with the cavalry officer Count Vronsky, leaves her husband and son, and is shut out of the society she lived in. Beside her story runs that of Konstantin Levin, a landowner who loves Kitty Shcherbatskaya, marries her, farms his land and searches for the meaning of his life. The novel opens with its famous sentence on happy and unhappy families.

No. 28 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s fourth part, The nineteenth-century novel, prints Anna Karenina whole in two volumes, Parts One to Four and Parts Five to Eight, in the translation of Constance Garnett (1901). The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Tolstoy and the Russia that followed the emancipation of the serfs, and explanatory notes on Russian names and ranks, the society of the two capitals, the farming questions Levin argues over, and the religious questions of his search.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
lead: Dostoevsky’s last novel, of a murdered father and his three sons, in Constance Garnett’s translation, in two volumes.
description: The Brothers Karamazov was Fyodor Dostoevsky’s last novel, published in the Russian Messenger in 1879 and 1880 and as a book in 1880, a few months before his death at St Petersburg in January 1881. He wrote it after the death of his three-year-old son Alyosha in 1878, and after a visit that summer to the monastery of Optina Pustyn and its elder, Father Ambrose. He meant it as the first part of a longer work he did not live to write.

Fyodor Karamazov, a dissolute landowner, has three sons: Dmitri, a passionate former officer, Ivan, an intellectual and doubter, and Alyosha, a novice in the town monastery under the elder Zosima. Dmitri and his father are rivals for the same woman, and when the father is found murdered, Dmitri is arrested. The novel holds Ivan’s poem The Grand Inquisitor, his argument from the suffering of children, and the life and teaching of Father Zosima.

No. 29 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s fourth part, The nineteenth-century novel, prints the novel whole in two volumes, Parts One and Two, and Parts Three and Four with the Epilogue, in the translation of Constance Garnett (1912). The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Dostoevsky’s last years and the Russian Church of the elders, and explanatory notes on Russian names and forms of address, the monastery and its ways, the law and the trial, and the Scriptures and saints the novel quotes.

title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
author: Mark Twain
lead: Mark Twain’s novel of the boy Huck and the runaway slave Jim on a raft down the Mississippi.
description: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born in Missouri in 1835 and grew up at Hannibal on the Mississippi. He was a printer, a river pilot until the Civil War closed the river, a miner and a newspaperman in Nevada and California, and took the name Mark Twain from the leadsman’s call for two fathoms of water. Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, a sequel to The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, appeared in London in December 1884 and in New York in February 1885.

Huck Finn, the son of the town drunkard, escapes his father by faking his own death and meets on an island in the river Jim, Miss Watson’s slave, who has run away rather than be sold down the river. The two go down the Mississippi on a raft, meeting feuding families, two swindlers who call themselves a duke and a king, and the towns of the river, while Huck struggles with what he has been taught about helping a slave to escape.

No. 30 of Lérins Classics, in the collection’s fourth part, The nineteenth-century novel, prints the novel whole, from the first American edition of 1885, as Twain wrote it, its language unaltered, with E. W. Kemble’s illustrations. The Editors of the Mere Catholicity Project add a new introduction on Twain, the river and slavery in the Missouri of his boyhood, and explanatory notes on the dialects of the book, life on the river, and the law and customs of slavery.
